speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the opposition of the last government to the bombing in North Viet Nam, and in view of the statement made by the Secretary General of the United Nations as
September 24, 1968

reported in this morning's press, is the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the government considering taking the initiative in proposing to the General Assembly the kind of resolution the Secretary General has suggested?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: UNITED NATIONS
subtopic: VIET NAM-DE-ESCALATION OF MILITARY ACTIVITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have read, and so have the government, the statement by the Secretary General of the United Nations in favour of stopping the bombing in Viet Nam and also his opinion that there may well exist a majority in the assembly for this view.
We ourselves, as the government has expressed on a number of occasions, consider a halt to the bombing as one of the essential first steps which will have to be taken by both sides to the conflict. In our view, a balance would have to be kept in such appeal if it were to be made. A resolution calling only for a halt in the bombing without stressing the obligation on the other side to contribute significantly to military de-escalation would not seem to reflect what has to be done by both sides if peace is to be restored.

maintopic: UNITED NATIONS
subtopic: VIET NAM-DE-ESCALATION OF MILITARY ACTIVITIES
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In view of the position of the Secretary General, which has been repeated many times, and in view of the position taken by the former prime minister which he stated once or twice-I am speaking from memory but I am sure I am not misrepresenting him-is the Secretary of State for External Affairs now saying to the house that he is opposed to a resolution such as that suggested by U Thant, and that he will take no steps to deal with it at the general assembly?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: UNITED NATIONS
subtopic: VIET NAM-DE-ESCALATION OF MILITARY ACTIVITIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the position of the Canadian government would, I think, depend on whether this sort of action would contribute to the end of the war in Viet Nam. The Secretary General has expressed his view and it is one that we would certainly look at seriously. We would want to be satisfied, however, that it would help to facilitate the peace negotiations that we hope are underway now.

maintopic: UNITED NATIONS
subtopic: VIET NAM-DE-ESCALATION OF MILITARY ACTIVITIES
speechtext: A further supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Would one be justified in thinking that because the ambassador of the United States at the United Nations has expressed opposition to the Secretary General's suggestion the Department of External Affairs in Canada is not willing to support it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER PROCEDURAL CHANGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my first words may I express my thanks to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for his support in this regard. I should like to reiterate that I do not at this time intend to set before the house the detailed changes the government will be proposing. I wish to take the occasion of the introduction of this motion to give the house some idea of the underlying propositions which the government is considering in connection with the change in the standing orders of the house and give some indication of the various areas of the standing orders which we would like to be changed for the purpose of better facilitating the house business.
I believe it has become a truism that in recent years parliament, not only in Canada but in Great Britain, has been doing badly, it has been the subject of a great deal of criticism. When analysed, the reasons for that criticism appear to be threefold: First, the demeanour with which we carry on our parliamentary business; second, the delays created in turning legislative intention into law and, third, the failure on the part of members to examine in depth the proposals which come before us.
With regard to the first of these criticisms, the question of demeanour or the manner in which we carry out the functions of the house,
I do not believe that even the most Draconian of rules or the greatest martinet of a speaker could possibly bring about any change or improvement. It remains an individual responsibility of the members as to the manner in which they approach their conduct in the chamber. But with respect to the second and third of these criticisms, the fact that we take too much time and that we do not go deeply enough into the business of the house, these seem to me to be areas in which we can take

Consideration of Procedural Changes collective responsibility, and indeed those are the two areas in which as an underlying theme the government feels changes should be made to the rules of the house.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
I think the first thing to be said about those two criticisms is that, at least to a degree they are contradictory. If we are to put more business through the house in a shorter period of time, obviously it will be impossible to go more deeply into each individual item. It was really to overcome this contradiction that the government proposed to put more work, and therefore more responsibility, into the standing committees system of the house.
If all business must at all times pass through a single pipe line-that is to say, this chamber-it is obvious that slowing down the flow in that pipe line by examining with greater scrutiny the individual details will impair the ability to get more tasks done. But if, as the government will propose to the special committee, we put the most detailed aspects of our work-for example, the detailed scrutiny of the estimates or the clause by clause examination of legislation- into the functional standing committees, then the flow will have been broken up into three, four or more pipe lines and a stoppage in one will not necessarily be a stoppage in all.
The dissatisfaction of the public with the manner in which we have conducted our business in the past was reflected in the past two parliaments in efforts made to bring about changes in our procedures. We in this parliament are the beneficiaries of the work of earlier parliamentary committees and also of the accumulated experience of this house in working with the provisonal rules which have been in effect in recent years and which have been carried on until the start of the session after Christmas.
By the committee which this resolution proposes, therefore, we have the opportunity and indeed the responsibility to bring to completion the changes which were proposed in those previous sessions and some of the changes which were carried out provisionally. From these general propositions I would like to move to a more specific consideration of the responsibilities of the house.
The fundamental duties of the house can be stated to be at least three. First, to authorize the imposition of taxation or, to put it in the jargon of parliamentary language, the business of ways and means.

Consideration of Procedural Changes

maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER PROCEDURAL CHANGES
speechtext:
Is this the order of
importance?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER PROCEDURAL CHANGES
speechtext:
I point out to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) that I do not know whether it is a principle his party would follow, but it is one that this party will follow, that on the whole we should not spend the money before we have it. Second, to authorize the expenditure of revenues so obtained by taxation-that is called the business of supply, the appropriation out of the public funds of moneys for government purposes-and third, to enact changes in our general public law, that is, those parts of our general public law other than those two financial aspects, which for the purposes of my remarks I would like to refer to as the ordinary legislative business.
The remarks with which I should like to begin in more detail relate to the business of supply, because essentially it is the question of supply which provides the anatomy of the parliamentary year. It is the bringing down of the estimates, dealing with the estimates and their subsequent voting, which to a very great degree determines the character the session will take. At the present time the items of expenditures proposed by the ministry- that is to say, the estimates-are examined by a committee of the whole house known as the committee of supply.
To provide those generally opposed to the ministry with opportunities to attack the ministry and to criticize its policies, the motion that the Speaker leave the chair to go into committee of supply has been made debatable on a fixed number of occasions. Each of these debates is limited to two days, always a Monday and the following Tuesday, and the provisional rules which hitherto were followed permitted a debate on four such occasions, making a total of eight days.
This meant that during each normal session the opposition could raise, by means of an amendment, four specific subjects on which it wanted a debate and a decision, entailling either an expression of confidence or nonconfidence by the house. Once a group of estimates has been given to the committee of supply they are gone over, item by item, by the entire membership of the house. Under the 1962 version of the standing orders there was no time limit stipulated for this item by item consideration. Under the provisional version the time limit of 30 days was prescribed for all the business of supply except the final supplementary estimates.

The importance of the business of supply is clear. First, it is one of the ways in which the house can assert the constitutional principle that a ministry is responsible to the house both in relation to its general conduct and the detail of its administrative work. Second, the business of supply, particularly the debates on supply motions, provides the opposition with an opportunity to bring before the house matters which may be of importance but which may not for the moment have been included in the government's program. Third, the business of supply provides members with an opportunity to examine, to comprehend and to influence the executive work of the various departments and agencies.
There has been criticism of the practices we have followed in dealing with supply. The criticism of the present practices seems to centre around three major points. First, it is said that the committee of supply is too cumbersome for the intensive study of the items in the estimates. Members are inclined to give speeches rather than to examine. Ministers often, rather than dealing with the questions as they are put, wait until the end and give a long reply which in itself becomes a long speech, which in turn may not be satisfactory to the questioners. Some items, not necessarily the most important or controversial, monopolize the time and energy of members, while others are marched through in the dying hours of a session.
The second criticism is that the four supply motion debates, based as they are on the needs of an era when the house met only three or four months each year during the winter and spring, do not meet modern requirements. Ordinarily these debates are bunched together into the spring, perhaps in successive weeks, so that the opposition must expend its ammunition whether or not it has at the moment a good target. No notice of the amendment is given, so that the real issue on the matter can only be joined on the Monday evening of the debate.
The third and final criticism is that it is said the serious study of the estimates is not promoted when as much as a half or three quarters of the total proposed expenditure already has been approved through votes by way of granting interim supply. It was probably these considerations which entered into the thinking of the special committee on procedure in 1967 and 1968 when it included the following in the report tabled in the house on March 13, 1968; the passage to
September 24, 1968

which I am referring may be found in Votes and Proceedings for that year, at page 764:
Your committee believes that we should scrutinize carefully the possibility of bringing together the best in the Canadian and British practice relating to the business of supply in order to decide if the result would be more satisfactory than the system which now prevails in either country. On the one hand, we are not prepared to abandon the examination of the estimates before the money is voted; indeed we believe that a major defect of present Canadian practice in this regard is that we deal with expenditure items ex post facto. If this practice is continued we probably should simply convert the consideration of the estimates into the examination of general and continuing programs. On the other hand we do not think that the use of weeks of supply days as presently carried on exerts much control over ministers and departments or is of any genuine value to the opposition. The British practice, while it avoids discussion of the estimates items, has the great value that it permits the opposition to explore whatever shortcomings, either small or great, it detects in the policies and conduct of the ministry before supply is voted.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
The committee's observations, I would submit, Mr. Speaker, lead to two general conclusions: First, that the study of estimates should take place in the standing committees around April 1 of each year, that is to say, the date on which the fiscal year of the government commences; and second, that a specified number of days in each annual session should be made available to the opposition for debates on opposition motions, that is to say, on subject matters which are the specific choice of the opposition.
In its fifth report the committee proposed that the main estimates be referred to the standing committees as soon as they are tabled, that is to say, some time fairly early in February, if the house was not to find itself dealing with the estimates in the following autumn. It should therefore conclude its work on those estimates before the summer. Consequently, it seems reasonable to suggest that the standing committees should conclude their work before June 1.
In the United Kingdom, the days available to the opposition for its own motions are sometimes called supply days and they really parallel our supply motion days. Often, to avoid any suggestion that the supply days are confined either to the estimates as a whole or to specific items of expenditure, these days are referred to as allotted days or opposition days. Therefore, when I use that term that is the practice I will be referring to, namely, the days on which the opposition picks a subject matter, the subject matter not being confined to any specific item in the estimates.

Consideration of Procedural Changes
The special committee of this house which sat early this year and last year envisaged the annual sessions as beginning in the autumn. This would mean that some time before or after the Christmas recess, but not too soon after the votes on the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne which we just concluded, there should be a number of supply or opposition days so that the opposition could have the opportunity of stating its views on public questions of its choice.
On the other hand, the ministry is in need of getting interim supply before the start of each fiscal year. Therefore the opposition should have an additional number of days before the end of March. The number should take into consideration the fact that the debate and votes on the budget normally come in April, and therefore in the spring period there would be other opportunities to make this type of general observation.
Since the supply sought in the main estimates should be granted or denied before too great a part of the fiscal year has passed, that is to say, before the summer break, another set of opposition days should be planned for the months of April, May and June, and especially for late May and June, because of the absence from that period of other opportunities, such as the debate on the address and the budget, for the opposition to take the initiative on this type of matter. Moreover, because the reports prepared by the standing committees on estimates would be ready by June, it is conceivable that the opposition would select one or more of its opposition days specifically for the purpose of debating a report from a special standing committee on estimates which may be of particular interest.
One of the critical questions is how many supply or opposition days should be allotted to this purpose, and this is a question which is not easy to answer. I would suggest there is no particular number of any magical significance. For example, under the provisional rules there were eight supply motion days, but there were also under those rules 30 additional days for the examination of the estimates in committee of supply. On the other hand, at Westminster there is a total of 29 days, but there the current year's estimates are not studied intensively, as would be possible here in Canada.
It may be contended, of course, that there should be no time limits whatsoever, that is to say, that the debate on supply should continue until each and every member has been fully and finally satisfied with regard to his
September 24, 1968

Consideration of Procedural Changes questions on the estimates. However, the constitutional requirement is that the House of Commons be satisfied, and the House of Commons makes its decisions by majority votes. In other words, the standing orders should give the majority of the house opportunities to decide whether or not it supports the ministry. Here again the special committee, this time in its fifth report which was tabled on March 29, 1968, made this general observation with respect to the question of supply:
-the house should decide whether or not to grant supply at regular intervals so that (a) the opposition's opportunities to criticize are not concentrated in any one part ot the year and (b) the ministry is not distracted by constant uncertainty about supply.
I would submit that the opposition should have as many supply days as it needs, but it should not have the embarrassment-and I am taking advice in this regard from certain distinguished members on the occasion of their visit to Westminster-of having to use more days than it feels justified in using. The problem in stipulating this number of days in the rules, as I had the opportunity of stating in the throne speech debate, is that the maximum inclines to become the minimum. For example, an extra five or ten days, perhaps running on into July, are not particularly crucial for the government. Finding the best number of days really matters more to the opposition. They should have as many supply days as they need, but they should not have the embarrassment of having to use more days than they would feel justified in using. If that proposition is questioned, I would refer to some of the observations of the group which visited Westminster.
Another difficult problem concerns the significance of supply day motions from the standpoint of revealing whether or not the ministry continues to have the confidence of the house. If the question of confidence were clearly entailed in every vote on a supply day, the opposition might be made to appear overly zealous to bring on an election, and this might be politically embarrassing. Moreover, if the question of confidence were clearly entailed in every vote on a supply day, a minority government probably would be far less able to survive than under the present arrangements.

As to the advisability of having acting ministers, that is another possibility to be considered.

changes in standing orders, further suggestions which would improve the manner in which the house goes about its business and with which the government can co-operate.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that we have inherited in our parliamentary system of government an exceptional institution. It is exceptional by that ultimate standard, that it has been successful in providing effective government, at the same time providing protection of the rights of individuals. But even a casual examination of the history of the British system of parliamentary government reveals that its essential genius lies, it seems to me, not in the fact that one final set of proposals have been set down and followed thereafter but in its adaptability. Because procedures could be varied and have been varied from time to time, the institution is able to change with changing circumstances.
In this respect, Mr. Speaker, parliament may be likened to a living being, not a dead and ossified set of procedures established for all time but an evolving institution capable of growing and altering to meet the new demands of our changing society.
In this committee, therefore, we are establishing for this house and for our parliamentary institution another means of such growth, a source of adaptation of procedures that we have inherited to the demands of our new and increasingly complex age. It presents for us in the house both an opportunity and a challenge to make certain that we have tended carefully our great inheritance in our time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER PROCEDURAL CHANGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this party welcome this opportunity to discuss in this chamber as it should be discussed the question of the procedures under which this house carries on its business and maintains the great and noble character of the institution it has become and which I fervently pray it will continue to be. It is true, sir, that there is need for change, that there are, as the minister has said, certain obsolescences which have crept into our procedures. The characteristic of longevity is not to suggest that some of the principles, not so much the reflection of those principles but the principles themselves, should be eternal and with us forever. I might say that certain habits of the human race have continued. Adam and Eve started one which has continued quite acceptably up till the present time, so far as I am aware.
In connection with these proposals, Mr. Speaker, I am quite convinced from my discussions at various times in and out of the

Consideration of Procedural Changes house, both with members of my party and with members of other parties, that there are changes which will undoubtedly be acceptable to all. On the other hand, I am convinced from what I have seen and heard that there are changes that the government is going to propose which will not be acceptable. This is where we will part company from the government. This must necessarily be so, Mr. Speaker. The government and the opposition must, for the good of the country, approach the issue of the transaction of business in this house from a completely different viewpoint.
Take legislation, sir. Legislation is enacted on the advice and assent of the Senate and the House of Commons. Many governments, particularly this government, I feel, barely tolerate assent and are very unhappy about advice. This is one of the areas we must now approach in order to see to what extent the practices of this house can be enlarged to permit a greater measure of advice, change and adaptation by the house as a whole of government proposals.
Not for one minute would I ever suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the initiative must not at all times flow from the government. The purpose of government is to govern. In the kind of society in which we now live, and having in mind the responsibilities of members of this house on both sides-I speak now for those private members who sit behind the minister and on this side as well as for members of opposition parties-there is ample opportunity for members to participate to some extent in the legislative process once bills and other measures have been brought into the house. The proposals that we will make will have some connection with this idea.
When the government sees fit to introduce a measure and brings it to the stage of second reading, obviously it is a measure that has worked its way up from the bowels of the civil service, has received final approval so far as the government is concerned, and probably has political sex appeal. Once the bill comes to second reading it is a beloved child of the government. The government, as is the custom of all parents, will not tolerate any suggestion that there is any hint of imperfection or deformity in this child.
I think this has been one of the great difficulties in the legislative process. Too many times have too many statutes gone through this house without the government receiving those proposals that private members are well able to make and are probably
September 24, 1968

Consideration of Procedural Changes better qualified to submit than the civil service. Who better than the private member in close touch and communication with his constituents, the people of Canada, can consider and survey the impact of a legislative proposal, how that piece of legislation affects the people he represents, and how will it affect all the people of Canada? I think there is an opportunity in the legislative process, without to any extent at all impairing the initiative, prerogative and responsibility of the government, to permit this to be done.
During the last four years 210 statutes have been passed. Of these, if one excludes appropriation bills and new bills originally passed, 93 measures were in fact amending statutes. As I said the other day, no government, no group of people, can possibly cast their minds far enough ahead to prepare for all of the contingencies and eventualities which human life and its vicissitudes may bring about. However, Mr. Speaker, I suggest to you, not only as a member of the house but as one who, together with a great number of my colleagues, has spent years practising before the courts, that there are innumerable cases of statutes coming out of this parliament and out of provincial legislatures which are half-baked, ill-conceived, ill-prepared and which do not attain the object for which they are designed. This situation can be cured by giving the members of this house through various media which I hope will be suggested to this standing committee, an opportunity to put in a more concrete and eloquent way, a way which will receive some attention from the government, proposals which will better the legislation enacted by this parliament.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I suspect we all remember the story of the Procrustean bed and of the robber who placed his victims on it. If they were too long when he placed them on it he cut their feet off; if they were too short he had them stretched. That is often the type of legislation to come out of legislative bodies. It is much simpler to change the size of the bed. If we do that we shall obtain better legislation.
More consideration must be given to the views of individual members of this house. We must not permit the unique and difficult circumstances at present facing us to hasten our decision. I repeat and emphasize what I said earlier during the throne speech debate: we must not permit the government or any of its members to hasten us into a decision with regard to rule changes which will be designed 

primarily to fit the unusual circumstances existing at the present time.
Since last December, when the then prime minister, Mr. Pearson, indicated his intention of resigning his position, we have had no effective government. Some measures were passed, there was some attention to business, but we have had no real government. Much of the legislative backlog and consideration of estimates which awaits us derives from this fact. Because of the action or lack of action of the government of that time we went from crisis to crisis up to the end of last March. Under normal circumstances we should have returned after the Easter recess prepared to deal with the estimates and other legislative proposals then on the order paper. That did not happen, for obvious reasons.
Today we recognize the difficulties of the government. Because of a political decision made by the present Prime Minister and his supporters we find that we are now faced with an overloaded legislative program, many parts of which we recognize as being essential for the people of this country. That being so, we shall continue to give, as we have given, our utmost measure of co-operation despite the fact that the entire fault for our present circumstances lies on the shoulders of those who are on the government side of the chamber.

A similar situation prevailed in the longest session this parliament has ever known, the session of 1966-67, during which the house sat for almost 250 days and passed, I believe, 83 bills. A survey of them can be a very interesting exercise. Seventy eight of those 83 measures were each passed in one day. It took one day each for those measures to pass all stages, and in parliamentary terms one day is roughly equivalent to between four and four and a half hours. Five bills of that session took 80 days to pass. Those five bills included the decennial revision of the Bank Act, then two or three years overdue, the unification of the armed forces bill, f the old age security legislation, medicare and the transportation bill, each being lengthy and extremely controversial. Their passage involved significant and substantial legislative changes. As I say, they were long, difficult and complex bills and, if I am not mistaken, three or possibly four of them were never sent to a committee. The transport bill went to a committee, and though it took many days to pass throuh the house it would have taken
Sepiember 24, 1968	COMMONS
much longer if it had not first gone to a committee where amendments were proposed and accepted. While in its final form that bill was not the best that could have been produced by the house, its consideration in committee cut down the time of passage through the house.
The estimates went through in the time then allotted under the provisional standing orders. I think the government of that day must take the responsibility for the length of the session and for the fact that five measures, which were of great complexity and difficulty, took the time they did to pass through the house.
The same remark might well apply to our present situation. We shall be asked to deal with measures such as the omnibus amendments to the Criminal Code involving five isolated and difficult problems, any one of which ought to be the subject of a separate measure and every one of which involves the conscience and serious consideration of members of this house. Each of those amendments, as I say, ought to be included' in a separate measure.
The minister talks about the reform of the legislative process, and I agree with him. There is a lot of room for improvement. But,
I ask, in the name of heaven how can the minister and the government expect members of the house to consider briefly the second reading stage of a bill such as the omnibus amendments to the Criminal Code involving five important, difficult and controversial subjects, to say nothing of the 200 or 300 sections, which in a substantive or procedural way may deeply affect, if adopted, the lives and liberties of the people of Canada. That is the position. I do not know what the government will do. I do not know what the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) will propose. Is the matter to go to a committee and will witnesses be called? That is the sort of thing the select committee on procedure will need to look at earnestly and seriously.
I repeat the proposition I made. It is not good enough for members of this house, when approaching a study of the reform of the rules and regulations which govern our conduct in this house, to consider reforms with minds oriented only toward a consideration of the difficulties which face us at present. I hope the minister and the government agree with me. We must take the long view.
What will be the situation two years from now or three years from now? The Prime Minister called an election and we are now

Those are the general comments I wish to make. There are some particular areas I wish to cover. Other members of our party may have other comments to make. I wish to deal with the question of committees. I agree that there is a place for committees in this house. More use might be made of them, though not to the extent that use is made of them in the United States.
In my hand I have reports of two United States committees, the very prestigious foreign affairs committee of the Senate and the joint economic committee of Congress which has members from the House of Representatives and the Senate. The latter committee comes up with proposals which are issued in a statement similar to or the equivalent of a white paper tabled by the Minister of Finance in parliament. It is probably given even greater consideration than the report of the economic consultative committee established by the President. I do not think it is part of our parliamentary tradition that this should be done. However, I believe we could go a lot farther than we do today.

Committees must not be frustrated by a refusal on the part of chairmen to bring committee reports into the house. Committees must not be frustrated by the refusal of the government to call them together and set them in motion so as to carry out the terms of reference assigned to them. In this connection I need only refer to the public accounts committee which is faced with the formidable task of dealing with three annual reports by the Auditor General before the session is over.
Again, a committee having made a report and it having been brought before the house, there should be reasonable opportunity given for the report to be debated. The government is not obliged to accept it, of course, but if a committee has struggled with the problem placed before it and brought a report forward there should certainly be an opportunity, within reasonable limits, of debating it. These things, plus the establishment of reasonable budgets for committee activities, are essential if committees are to do part of the work of the house within the terms proposed by the minister.

I agree we have now reached a stage where certain aspects of our legislative program are not dealt with most effectively and efficiently in the house. Committees can play a considerable role. The committee on estimates is an apt illustration. But not for one moment do I entertain the idea that this house should at any time or under any circumstances delegate to a committee of the house the decision-making power which can only reside here in this chamber.

maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER PROCEDURAL CHANGES
speechtext:
Similarly, when a committee has made its report it is the house which must decide. Again, responsibility cannot be abdicated. I agree that there is an inquisitorial and investigative process which can best be discharged through the medium of the committee system. I agree that by using the committee system hon. members can add to their knowledge, provided, of course, that other facilities are made available to them. A while ago the minister said we should not spend our money before we get it. I can assure him we shall not engage any research staffs until we have seen the estimates.
Hon. members undoubtedly have an opportunity to become more knowledgeable when they can sit across the table from a minister and direct questions to him, provided, of course, that the minister is a little more informative than he is in the house, and when they have the opportunity to examine expert witnesses. I am confident that in these circumstances members come back to this house better prepared for a crisper, more intelligent and, I would venture to suggest, shorter debate directed to the principles, and it is to the principles that this house should always be directing its attention. We ought surely to make use of the committee system but we must stop short of giving to committees rights which only this house can exercise.
I still entertain the utmost hope of achieving a measure of reform along the lines I have suggested. I must admit, though, that I am a lot more careful now in this regard than I was a year ago. The authoritarian trend which this government has indicated, its almost grotesque obsession with secrecy, must place a responsibility on all members of the opposition parties to be most careful when it comes to giving up rights which are essential for the preservation of this institution and for the protection of the rights of the Canadian people.
We talk about the question period. On that score I would say to the hon. gentleman: we

all accept the fact that ministers of the crown have multifarious duties and that it may be necessary for them on occasions to be elsewhere employed in the business of the country. The government has the right to say that certain ministers will not be present on certain occasions. But we would strongly oppose any suggestion that, unilaterally, the government should decide that certain ministers would be absent on certain days. This could mean that if a crisis occurred on one of those days when a minister was not here the house would be obliged to wait until he returned.

We observe with concern that government grows ever stronger and stronger-and government is more and more coming to mean the office of the prime minister. Add to this the implications of the discovery by creators of television public affairs programs that politics and politicians can be subjected to treatment in such a way as to project an element of entertainment and there is yet another reason for our concern. The image which appears on the television screen can be so manipulated and distorted that it is sometimes more art than nature.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
More and more frequently this new toy will emphasize the emergence of personalities, the cult of the individual, and somehow we will have to learn to live with it. But it does violence to the basic principle of parliamentary democracy. We must then find ways and means to seek out and bring forward counterbalancing forces to check and control the startling expansion of the Prime Ministry, an institution occupied by an individual but rapidly becoming an office which no one person is capable of understanding or directing, no matter what his qualifications.
The United States wisely provided a system of checks and balances by keeping the executive separate from the legislative branch. We do not agree with their system but they have these checks and balances. They may have made too great a fetish of it, but certainly, Mr. Speaker, the checks and balances which the private members of the opposition parties must have, retain and expand in order to keep watch on this government must not be lost in the type of parliamentary reform which is considered in the committee.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER PROCEDURAL CHANGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the motion that is now before the house and I did not mind the way in which Your Honour turned the tables on me and named me as the seconder of it.
I might say that not only do we agree with the motion but I agree with many things that the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) said during the course of his speech. In fact I feel I must say to him that it is a better speech than it would have been if he had made it before we had several consultations among the house leaders. It struck me that he paid attention to some of the counterproposals that were made by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), the hon.
Consideration of Procedural Changes member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau), and myself. He did not accept all of our suggestions. There was one in particular, related to the question period, on which he did not accept our position, but generally speaking I think the minister's speech has demonstrated already the value of consultation in this field.
I welcome also the portions of the speech of the hon. member for Peace River in which he emphasized the problem that faces us with respect to time and the necessity of our including, in any changes in the rules that we make, full protection for the rights of all members of the House of Commons.
It is often said, Mr. Speaker, but I do not think we can repeat it too often, that the rules of this house are parliament's business, not the government's. The government is recognizing that fact by placing this motion before the house and by asking an all-party committee to deal with the rules of the house. We in turn as members of the opposition have an obligation not only to criticize the proposals that may be made by the government but to make proposals ourselves and to accept the responsibility of working out jointly rules and procedures that will make for the best operation of the House of Commons.
In that vein, Mr. Speaker, there are some specific suggestions that I want to make in a few minutes. Some of them may not be popular in all quarters but I think we do have to get down to the serious business of dealing with our rules. However, before I do so there are a few conceptions or misconceptions about parliament that I think ought to be cleared up.
In the first place, I think it should be emphasized that bringing in new rules, no matter how good or how far reaching they may be, is no substitute for good legislation, and I say to the government that I have a little bit of concern-perhaps more than a little bit-that it is a technocratic kind of government. It is going to foster changes in the rules. It is going to reorganize the departments of government. It is going to come along with different ways of doing things, but good legislation of substance is down at the bottom of the list. That is not good enough. It is not good enough to try to substitute changes in the rules for good legislation.
The other side of the coin, Mr. Speaker, is equally valid. Making changes in the rules is no substitute for good performance on the part of members on both sides of the house. Just as we will not let the government use the rules as an excuse for not getting its
September 24, 1968

Consideration of Procedural Changes business through, so we should not use the rules as an excuse for not being good members, for not attending to our business, for not being in our places, for not making proposals worthy of the consideration of parliament. Rules are important, but more important than rules are the legislation the government brings in and the performance of members on both sides of the house.
A second point I would like to make is one that arises out of a criticism that we often read in the press. It is a criticism that a number of members made during the course of the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. It has to do with the question of talk, of speech-making in parliament. There are times when our critics on the outside, and some on the inside, speak as though talking is a crime, as though making speeches is something that should not happen in parliament. Well, Mr. Speaker, there is such a thing as too much talk. There is such a thing as burying important business in a flood of words. I said to one interested person a day or two ago, when some comments were made about the length of the throne speech debate and that eight days were maybe longer than it needed to be, that when I first came here the throne speech took a full month. That was back in the early and middle 1940's. My friend, who had been an observer of the scene in those days, replied that Mackenzie King liked it that way, that by talking and talking in the throne speech debate members did not bother him about the business of the country.
I agree that there is such a thing as too much talk, but let us not allow the press, or anyone in this house, to get away with the thought that the main purpose of changing the rules is to cut down on or eliminate the right of free speech.

maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER PROCEDURAL CHANGES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER PROCEDURAL CHANGES
speechtext:
Thank God for free speech. It is the heart and the essence of democracy. Much as I am used to the formalities that we go through when we go over to the Senate to open a session of parliament, I always enjoy hearing Mr. Speaker claim from the representative of the crown the right of free speech for all members of parliament. It is when people do not have free speech, when matters cannot be discussed, that you lose democracy, that you have authoritarianism, that you have dictatorship. Free speech is something that we should have, and in any attempt to reform the rules of parliament let us not think that 
we are doing something valuable just because we cut down on the length of time we spend in this house.
I want to say also that the notion that using time is a crime or mistake does not always hold up. It is important that we use our time wisely; it is important that we use it well. But the implication I get from some criticism of parliament is that we should so organize our rules that we can do the year's work in two or three months and then go home, go about our other business or what-have-you. I think that is wrong and is not in keeping with the whole purpose of parliament. As a matter of fact, authoritative writers on the problems of parliament, its rules and procedures, over the decades have said that the important thing we must do when we talk about time is not simply to aim at saving time but to aim at making the best use of the time we have.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
There is another misconception I would like to clear up, Mr. Speaker, and I hope I am demonstrating my impartiality in this field. Some of my hon. friends opposite may not believe it but I think it is no crime for the government to try to get its legislation through parliament. After all, that is what governments are elected for. They are elected because the people support their policies. The people expect them to come to parliament with legislation to implement those policies and to do their best to get that legislation through.
I think we who are members of the opposition should not completely prevent legislation getting through. On the other hand, it is no crime for an opposition to attempt to stop a government putting through something that it disagrees with or something which the opposition feels has been hastily conceived and is not really good for the country. In other words, I am perhaps spelling out in another way what I had in mind when I talked about the right of free speech, namely, that the essence, the genius, of this place is that it is a place where there is equality on both sides. It is a place where the cut and thrust of debate is the basic rule, because it is out of the cut and thrust of debate that the government tries to get its legislation through with the opposition having the right to check it as it goes through and to keep the government from doing things that are wrong for the country. That is the democratic process and through it we can achieve the best for our times.

I should like to go on to say a word about tradition in so far as it affects the rules of parliament. There are some respects in which the traditions that are behind us are extremely good and must be respected, I would go so far as to say, to the end of time. I have in mind traditions which have to do with the right of free speech, traditions which have to do with the equality of the members on the floor of the House of Commons, traditions which have to do with the right of opposition members to expect the cabinet ministers to be present to answer questions in respect of their policies and their administration.
I think of the traditions we have about debate which divide it into various stages of time. We know that a rule could be devised whereby a government proposal would be debated once and that would be it. But our tradition says no, that it is better to have a first look at it, that it is a good idea to decide on it in principle, that then it should be looked at in detail and that after all that there should be another look at it. I go along with the President of the Privy Council in respect of some of the changes he wishes to make in that regard, but I make the point that there are some traditions like those centred around the right of free speech and the general process for the passing of legislation which are mighty good.
I believe all of us in this chamber have the right to be very proud of being members of this kind of an institution. We do not need to enhance our own position by making comparisons with other types of legislative bodies. I think, however, that we have inherited from our political progenitors one of the best kinds of legislative bodies. I think the essence of it is sound. I believe we would be making a mistake if we tampered with that essence and that we would do well to retain the heart and core of it.
On the other hand, there are times when tradition can hamper us. I think there is one area in which this is the case. The President of the Privy Council alluded to it today. I refer in particular to the trappings we have built up around the voting of supply and around the question of ways and means. It is not necessary to indulge in a treatise on history to remind hon. members that the British parliamentary system originated in an era when the King was out to get all the money he could get out of the barons. The barons, who later had to delegate some of their authority, were trying to prevent the King getting the money he wanted. So parliament

Consideration of Procedural Changes became largely involved in a test over this one question. Hence we had secretive types of supply and ways and means committees to discuss this kind of thing without the monarch looking on.
The result is that we have encrusted around our supply and ways and means machinery traditions which I do not think fit the 1960's or the 1970's. Even the committees that bear these names may be absolete. The struggle today is not a struggle between subjects and a king who is trying to obtain money for purposes they do not know very much about. The struggle today has shifted considerably. It is a struggle between the executive and parliament as a whole. It is also a struggle between points of view; it is a struggle among parties. I believe our own machinery should be adjusted to meet this situation. I shall come to that in a little more detail when I get down to the suggestion I intend to make.
I think it is becoming obvious that one of the areas where we must make the greatest reform is the way in which we handle the voting of supply and the providing of money. I accept the proposition, stated today so effectively by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), that we must keep control of the purse strings and that if we let go our control over the spending of money we let go our control over the government. But I shall still stand here and utter what to some people will appear to be heresy. I no longer think the voting of supply is the main business of parliament.
I have heard it uttered from this side of the house a good many times that supply is the main business of parliament, and I expect it will be uttered in the course of this debate. The business of supply is important just as the control of the purse strings is important, but today the whole field of legislation and policy, what we should do for our people from the cradle to the grave, what we should do about the problems, all the way from under the sea to outer space, which face us, calls for a consideration which surely anyone will admit is just as important as the voting of supply and I think even more important. I believe that the time has come when we must find a way by which the voting of supply, the voting of expenditures of which we must approve, can be handled a little more routinely so that we have more time to focus our attention on new policies for the new problems of our times.

There is nothing new about the suggestions I am making under the general heading of the word "tradition". There are some things about our traditions which I think are so eternally good that I hope we have them to the end of time. But because we value our free speech and the cut and thrust of debate, as well as all the other things that are part of democracy, does not mean that we must retain forever a system of voting money which came out of a time in history that has long since been left behind.
Having spent a little time in clearing away what I think are some of the misconceptions which I believe surround this house and its procedures I should like to come now to the specific matters to which I think our committee should address itself.

But I would like the committee to address itself to the main problem, on which I am sure we all agree, and the hon. member for Peace River confirmed this. That main problem is time.
I would be the last one to argue that dollars and cents are a satisfactory yardstick in this area, but at least it is a suggestion. I remind hon. members that in the first years of confederation the federal government's budget was of the order of $20 million. The annual budgets are now $10 billion. speechtext:
We
do not have to have that kind of rule today. You cannot multiply 65 sitting days by 50 in a 365-day year. So the problem is there, the problem of time, and we have simply got to do something about it.
Another way to look at the problem is to think of the various departments and consider the government as it is today. In 1860 there were questions of railways, canals and telegraph lines, agriculture and colonization, the Post Office and things like that, but today the federal government touches every area of life.
I mentioned Mackenzie King's name a few minutes ago. I am sure that if he were to come back, or if he is looking at things through the spiritual telescope he is reported to have, he would be flabbergasted by the amount of work we have to do today. He would probably say, "You should keep the throne speech going for 30 days and let the government run the business." That is the situation today, and the amount of work we have to do will become even greater in the future. If this is the case, if our problem is time and to get done in 12 months the amount of work that faces us, what are we going to do about it? There are a great many little details we can go over, but I want to consider two general things and then reject one and accept the other. One general way to deal with a lot more business in the course of the same amount of time, in other words, to deal
September 24, 1968	COMMONS
with 50 times as much business in the same 12 months, is to cut down the time spent on every item, to cut down speeches from 40 to 30 to 20 to 10 minutes, to cut down speeches in committee of the whole to 5 minutes. We could do all kinds of things. We could cut down the time spent dealing with bills to one or two days. We could cut down the question period. This is one way to do it, that is, cut down the amount of time spent on each item of business, each bill, each resolution, each matter parliament has to deal with. Obviously, I do not think that is the way to do it.
We have this explosion of business, and if we are aware of the fact that we have a great deal more to do now than members had 20 years ago, let alone 100 years ago, there are three other things we could do. I press these three things and, as is usual in my way of putting things, there may be some subheadings.
In the first place, I think we must learn to delegate a good deal of our work to committees of the house. We cannot go on forever dealing with 50 to 100 times as much work as we had and do it all on the floor of the house. I think we have to strengthen our committees in various ways which I want to suggest. We must delegate more work to our committees, and having given more work to them we must place some confidence, trust, and respect in them.
I know that one idea I have about committees has not yet commended itself to members generally, but I press it again. I believe that committees at certain times of the year should be given the centre of the stage and therefore parliament as a whole should adjourn for a week out of a month or for a couple of weeks every six weeks or so and let the committees meet and deal with the many problems referred to them. As I say, they should be given the centre of the stage. I think there are times when committees should be parliament.
I think also, Mr. Speaker, that when committees have dealt with matters, whether the estimates or detailed studies of bills, that work should not be duplicated on the floor of parliament. I accept the proposition of the hon. member for Peace River that in all cases the final decision should be made here, but as for this business of sending the estimates to committee, having them gone over in great detail and then having them come back to committee of supply and gone over again- well, we can do it if we want to, but I do not think it is a good use of time.

I think the same thing about bills. If a complicated bill like the broadcasting legislation, the armed forces unification bill or the Canada Pension Plan has gone to a committee and had a good, thorough going over by that committee, we should not repeat the same process here.
I like this suggestion made by the President of the Privy Council-I forget whether it was originally his or whether we worked it out in our sessions-that we should bring back to life what was once known as the report stage. If that report includes a reference to some things that were contentious, to some changes that were made, let the debate in the house be limited. Let it zero in on those particular points. I have no doubt some committees have operated that way. I have had the privilege of working on some committees where this was not the case, such as the old age security committee of 1950 and the Canada pension committee of a few years ago. I think hon. members who are here now and

Consideration of Procedural Changes who were here then will realize that we did have a say in the making of that report. 1 recognize that this kind of thing can happen, but I think it happened because we have left the committees in a downgraded position. No matter what they do, it is done all over again back here. I think we should put them in the centre of the stage. We should not duplicate their work. We should give the members of those committees the research assistance which is being talked about so that they can do a good job. I also think-the hon. member for Peace River said this and I agree with him-that it should be clearly understood that the reports of committees will all be dealt with back on the floor of the house.
When a committee deals with bills or with estimates they come back and certainly they have to be dealt with here, but if it deals with a problem it has been investigating, such as birth control or breathalizers, the report may come back and there may be no further discussion on it. You do not strengthen committees by making them smaller, giving them new names, giving them research assistance and so on, if you still leave them in an inferior position. I am always happy to express my respect for what they do at Westminster. I confess that last year when I was over there with the committee, although I thought I knew all that was going on over there I was amazed at the degree to which they have got legislation off the floor of the house and into their committees upstairs. Their committees meet in rooms which are set up like the House of Commons itself and they do things in the same formal way that we do here, but it is actually possible at Westminster for legislation to go through all the stages without ever being discussed on the floor of the house itself. This is also what happens to estimates.
Let me say that there is a safeguard. If a certain number of members-I think it is ten-insist that a bill come back to the floor, this is done. I am not advocating we go that far, but I am saying that if we have 50 times as much work to do as did the members of the first parliament of Canada we have to do something about the problem of time. As I say, one of the ways is to upgrade the work of the committees, taking into consideration the various suggestions I have made.
The second suggestion that I make involves the use o a phrase which was always anathema to my good friend, the hon. Gordon

Churchill, the former member for Winnipeg South Centre, namely, "allocation of time". I have a great deal of respect for the views about parliament of my former neighbour, and when one speaks of these things one feels he is still here. For all we know he may be in the gallery listening to the debate.
I support allocation of time, because I do not like closure. Closure is a bad word which we all dislike, but I know of no more effective form of closure than unlimited debate. When you spend all of the time or most of the time in a year on the question of a flag you cut off the possibility of discussing medicare in that session. That type of closure is just as effective as if the government brought in the use of the rule. I think it is not a denial of free speech, it is not a denial of the democratic process, for us to find a way whereby we can agree to the amount of time that will be given to one subject so we can go to another. There is just too much to do for us to spend all our time on one subject.
I am glad we left 15-A out of the provisional rules to which we have agreed for the balance of this year. In fact, perhaps I might be forgiven for telling the house that I proposed at a meeting of the house leaders that we leave out 15-A. I did so as a form of conciliation in which I was engaged at that time. I did so because I do not think it is a satisfactory rule for the allocation of time. I think it can be improved on. It has to be something that will be worked on in advance as an all-party proposition, in the context of a parliament which is going well because people feel they are getting their say in committees, are getting good legislation, and have a sufficient number of opportunities to speak on the floor. These are the kind of things, all wrapped together, which I think we have to do.
As I said, I had three things I wanted to give by way of suggestions about this time problem, but the time allocated to me is running out so I had better get on. I have already said I think we have to learn to delegate more of our work to committees. I want to add this postscript to what I said. If we do not delegate work to committees and if we do not allocate our time, what will happen is that we will in effect be delegating our work to the bureaucracy. We will delegate it right out of parliament. On another occasion I will quarrel over the answer which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) gave to me today about an order in council passed last April
September 24, 1968	COMMONS
which put into effect certain customs duties- and the order in council actually says this-at the level at which they would have been had parliament passed a resolution which was on the order paper. When parliament did not deal with the matter, we forced the bureaucracy to find some way to act without us. I think this was an improper order in council.
However, the point I am making at the moment is that if we do not find ways and means of dealing with our problems by improving the committee structure and by allocating our time for the debate of various issues we can be sure that the public service- it is a tremendous service of which we are very proud but it is not elected; we are the elected people-will take over and will run the business of the country.
The other suggestion I make is-and here I will use a word which may not be in the dictionary-that we have to "calendarize" our parliamentary year. The committee on procedure of the last parliament suggested this, and the President of the Privy Council has already referred to it today. We proposed that a session should begin in the autumn and wind up in June or July, with certain deadlines along the way. I think this is all tied in with the business of delegating work to committees and of allocating our time, but I think it has to be done.
The trouble with our way of doing things for the last quarter of a century that I have been around here is that the only real deadlines we seem to have are Christmas, Easter, or some hoped for prorogation date. This does not make good sense. What happens is that a lot of legislation piles up, and then we push billions of dollars worth of estimates and all sorts of legislation through simply because it has to be done so we can get home for Christmas, Easter or a summer vacation. This is not rational. I think that surely we have the capacity, the wit and the ability to plan a year, even if it has to be within limits. I know there are emergencies for which the program must be changed.
I would put a firm limit on the time when the estimates have to be passed. They have done it in Britain and they have not denied free speech over there. We have to "calendarize" our year and we have to have certain periods when we will deal with legislation or estimates if we are to deal with them after they come back from the committees. We also have to have certain periods in which to deal with budgets. It would be good for the country and good for parliament if we worked on

As I said, I have avoided getting into a lot of details because I think the main problem is the question of time. I repeat, let us keep the traditions that we have and that are worth keeping. On the other hand, let us not be bogged down by traditions that have no relevance or meaning in our times. On this problem of time let there be other suggestions, but I challenge anyone to state the problem any more forcibly than I have, namely, that the problem is time. Democracy is not a dead thing, it is living, and it will go on being changed and improved as time goes on. Our job, however, is not to worry about the changes to be made in the year 2000. Consideration of Procedural Changes make it possible for us to work more efficiently. The new procedure will have to strive-and that is what it must aim at-to increase the efficiency of the house, because often in the past the public and even the members of parliament have criticized the slowness, the inefficiency of the house or, often, the insufficient time available to deal with the business of the house.
At the same time-and that is the main point I want to raise today-this procedure should also enhance the prestige of members, in short emphasize their role as legislator and not as civil servant. I think that the former procedure considered the member mainly as a civil servant while he should normally be a legislator. I know it is difficult to develop and put forward a new procedure which will be faultless, but that is not a reason to attack the existing procedure, so as to enable parliament to do more in less time. That is why we are going to co-operate with the house leaders, to come to an agreement which will permit the development of a process enabling us to pass legislation faster and put forward more appropriate bills before the problems of our country get worse.
Thanks to our procedure, I noticed in the past-despite my little experience in this house-that parliament often found solutions to very serious problems, but because of the slowness of procedure, these solutions were so long delayed that the problems were getting worse and worse.
The President of the Privy Council mentioned that our present procedure took too much time. He also made another remark which seemed to contradict the first one, namely that the members did not have the time necessary to study the legislation in depth, that they took too long. That is true. He is right about those two points but, on the other hand, there are reasons for that. If the honourable members are unable to study the legislation in depth, there is an explanation.
First, the member has to perform his legislative duty and, unfortunately, to act as a civil servant. He has to make inquiries, study reports and look into all the royal commissions the government has set up. He must also, from time to time, participate to the various parliamentary associations and, therefore, he has to take different trips.
He also has to examine all the briefs submitted by various groups. Some of them originate from members of Chambers of Commerce or various groups in the country. He also has to meet people and ascertain the work which is done, at the provincial level,

in the legislative field. He also has to do part of his research himself. He must be well informed in order to keep abreast of Canadian policy, and even the international policy. He must sit in the house and attend the various committee meetings. We say that if the new procedure is passed, committees will expand in future, they will become more important, more powerful and they will automatically require greater preparation on the part of the members.
This is my complaint. If we lack the time and if we devote too much time to routine procedure, we will not have any time left for consideration in depth. I will point out now what is mentioned in the Speech from the Throne with regard to the official opposition:
-So that the Official Opposition, to which we, in Canada, give formal recognition as a vital part of our democratic process, as well as the other parties in opposition, may be in a position to cope more effectively with the heavy load of action and decision each session must face, you will be asked to make new provision for the Official Opposition and the other parties in their parliamentary role.
It is all well and good to talk about passing a new procedure-and we are all for it-in order to expedite the business of the house, but we cannot ask the members to do more just with the tools available to them at the present time.
For instance, 1 would point out that the United States, our neighbours to the south, have 435 members of Congress and 100 senators, that is a total of 535 elected representatives. Those elected representatives are assisted by 8,000 employees who represent an average of 15 officials appointed for research or committee work for each member of Congress or the Senate. This system is intended to facilitate the role of the elected representatives as legislators in order that they may devote their time to the welfare of the population. Mr. Speaker, this leads me to say that our present procedure is antiquated-and we all agree on that-because we have come to the point where we want it altered, improved and modernized. Besides, we have too many civil servants to enforce our legislation but we do not have assistants, the tools, the civil servants or the scientists to help us prepare our legislation.
A member of the house must do all his office work, do his part as a member of the house in his constituency, prepare and control legislation in its various stages and attend committee meetings. However, he does not have the tools permitting him to act as a true
September 24, 1968	COMMONS
legislator, and that is why speeches in the house are often too long. I agree with the president of the Privy Council that the speeches are often too long, because they are badly prepared. We lack the necessary research personnel and we cannot do the work in depth, because we cannot do everything and still discharge our duties properly.
If we want the members of this house to act as legislators and statesmen, we must give them the necessary means. We have put particular emphasis on the passage in the Speech from the Throne which shows the intention of putting such means at the disposal of the opposition in order to allow its members to help the government when it presents good legislation, to help it in its legislative work and, at the same time, make constructive criticisms and express their own views.
My main point today is that our parliamentary procedure and rules will have to be amended in that direction. We will increasingly have to act as legislators instead of civil servants. Therefore, the new procedure will have to give all the members of this house, whether they sit on the left or on the right of the Speaker, the tools to act in their true legislative capacity.
