Mr. Speaker, there are a few matters to which I thought I might refer, some of which have not been dealt with. I crave the indulgence of the house to make observations regarding certain matters that I feel ought to be brought to its attention.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has said that no longer is supply of first importance for parliament. That view is not consistent, I submit, with the general acceptance of the principle that parliament must keep a firm hold on the pursestrings of the nation. All of us want to make parliament more effective; that has been my objective through the years. I spoke on this subject in 1965; on May 20 I stated that I believed in reform to meet changing conditions without in any way destroying the mission of this house.
There have been improvements, Mr. Speaker. The designation of yourself, sir, as the Speaker of the House for a second parliament was one of the most forward steps that has been made to bring about in this institution the assurance that in debate decorum shall be 29180-27
DEBATES	413
Consideration of Procedural Changes maintained and, above all, that the rights of members of parliament wherever they sit shall not be denied.
It cannot be emphasized too much, Mr. Speaker, that every member in this house, whether recently elected or not, whether a member of the privy council or not, must have the opportunity of placing before the house his views on behalf not only of his constituency but of his country as well. There is no more important debate that can take place in this house than the strengthening of this institution, without which freedom cannot survive. I do not say this by way of criticism, Mr. Speaker, but this afternoon the number of members present, 40 or 50, does not indicate that there is very general recognition of the necessity for maintaining the greatness and supremacy of this institution, for bringing about needed reforms while at the same time assuring that the great traditions of the past that preserved our freedom in two world wars shall be upheld. It was this institution, Mr. Speaker, that between 1914 and 1918 gave the lead. It was this institution that between 1939 and 1945 gave to the people of this nation that determination which brought about, in alliance with those who were associated with us, the freedom that is ours.
I am not here to say that members should be in the house, Mr. Speaker. But one of the major criticisms of this institution is that members are not in the house. No one is guiltless in this regard. People come into the gallery and when they come out exclaim: "What an institution this is! There was scarcely anyone in the chamber". And so they join that galaxy of criticism that has become so popular in this country and in other countries.
Criticism is not new, Mr. Speaker; it has been said over and over again over the years. Some there are who believe that they are actually the discoverers of the shortcomings of this parliament. Those who have that view do not read history. One has only to go back to 1661 when Samuel Pepys stated:
-how beastly things are carried on in parliament-they oppose all things that are moved by serious men. They are the most profane, swearing fellows that be heard in this life, which makes me think that they will spoil all and bring things ruinous about.
That was in the days of the Charleses. What about modern criticism, Mr. Speaker? I
September 24, 1968

Consideration of Procedural Changes think of Charles Dickens. He sat in the gallery of the House of Commons for years and he wrote of parliament:
This great dust heap of Westminster, laughing, coughing, oh-ing, groaning, a conglomeration of noise and confusion. No other place in existence is like it, excepting Smithfield on a market day, or a cockpit in all its glory!
The critics were about then, Mr. Speaker. I think of Robert Louis Stevenson, who said: "We all know about parliament and we are ashamed of it". We are now in the year 1968 and in Canada and in Great Britain the same criticisms are being made. Those who know not parliament feel the greater qualified to criticize the institution!
Major criticisms were mentioned this afternoon by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) and others who participated in tne debate. For example, it is alleged that we waste time. One would think that this institution was a meandering one in which legislation is not passed expeditiously. The critics contend that we talk too much. To use the words of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that is what parliament is for. We are not here for the purpose of turning out masses of legislation. We are here for the purpose of preserving the freedom of the average Canadian and for seeing to it that no man, however humble, is denied equal rights with others.
I speak as one, Mr. Speaker, who has been here for many years. I have been greatly impressed by the high quality of the members who have come to this their first parliament. It is always a matter of interest to listen to them as they make their maiden speeches, an experience that all of us who have been here in other parliaments have gone through. Nothing is more trying.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Over the years all our prime ministers have listened to new members and asked themselves, "Which one of these will ultimately become prime minister of the country?". I remember the man Mr. King designated. When Sir Wilfrid Laurier listened to Mr. Arthur Meighen speaking in 1908 he made the remark, "There's a future prime minister," and he was right. In 1912 Sir Robert Borden designated R. B. Bennett as a future prime minister, and so it has been all through the years. As young men come to this institution-I cannot say the same about women; we have only one woman member who is most distinguished-they give to this great body of the people hope for the future. They bring
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
new ideas, new concepts and new determinations.
How is it that a few days after parliament begins its deliberations many members disappear after orders of the day and house attendance is eroded? In 1791-92, in the parliaments of Upper and Lower Canada, if one looks at the rule book then in effect, as the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) has, one will find a rule saying that if a member is absent from the house and Mr. Speaker has noted the absence, the sheriff may be sent out to bring the delinquent before the bar of the house. When that was done once I am sure attendance thereafter was maintained.
This summer I was in the United Kingdom and visited the House of Commons at Westminster. I saw it first when I was on leave in November, 1916, when I heard the great Lloyd George make his first speech as prime minister of the United Kingdom. Then Britain was fearful and he raised up the nation. I saw that house during the days of Churchill. I saw Churchill in that chamber in November, 1916, following Gallipoli, when he was in disgrace. When I first met him I said to him, "I saw you first when you were in disgrace". His answer was, "Which time was that?". Later in 1940 he raised up the British people when they, and we, and other commonwealth countries were alone.
In the Canadian parliament I have heard since 1911 the greats throughout the years. Some will tell you that debating has disappeared in this chamber, that it is not what it was in the old days, and that is right. It is better. In my estimation the quality of debate, especially since the beginning years of the last war, has improved greatly in this house. I know that some say, "Let us cut down the time; let us pass our estimates and matters of controversy on to committees." I will go part way with that. The great danger of committees is this, sir. Many of those who give support to the principle in reality are comparing this institution with the congress of the United States, and it is different. There, in committee, all partisanship disappears. Their committees are all-powerful and you cannot get anywhere in those committees unless you have a great deal of seniority. Under that system a member who has been here for 28 years might head a committee. That seniority system is wrong because, as the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) said, it would destroy the efficiency and effectiveness of parliament.
September 24, 1968

It has often been suggested that we should imitate the United States system of government. I can never accept the concept of the republicanism of the United States being made a principle or yardstick for a parliament in the British tradition. It cannot be done.
In "The Decline of Legislatures" Lord Bryce has written:
Every traveller who. curious In political affairs, enquires in the countries which he visits how their legislative bodies are working, receives from the elder men the same discouraging answer. They tell him, in much the same terms everywhere, that there is less brilliant speaking than in the days of their own youth, that the tone of manners has declined,-
Today the President of the Privy Council mentioned the need to maintain a high degree of cultured demeanour and I interpolate to say that when I was in the British house recently there was a clash of opinion. They have no eggshell sentimentalities in that institution. The Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition clash. Not long ago the Leader of the Opposition, Mr. Heath, said in the British house, "I say to the Prime Minister, he cannot bully me," to which the Prime Minister replied, "the hon. member is in no danger, only a coward would do that," or words to that effect.
What would happen if those words were said in this institution? Why, I could just imagine the headlines all across this country.
Churchill's deputy prime minister of the war years, Attlee, formed a government which Churchill wanted to discredit. He said, looking at the front benches of the government, "It is a lousy government." Before the speaker could call him to order he went on to say, "I want to say that I was not using that term in an opprobrious way. It was purely a factual statement."
As I see it, with the exception of the prime minister, the leader of Her Majesty's loyal opposition-that is the correct designation, not the leader of the official opposition-and ministers making official statements, members should speak without a manuscript before them. Why waste the time of the house? If a speech is to be read, why do we not follow the United States system? If any here want to imitate the United States system why do they not adopt the procedure of the House of Representatives? There, when a member has a written out speech he says, "I should like to place my speech on the Congressional Record", and it is placed on the record. That saves time. If some hon. members here want
29180-27J
Consideration of Procedural Changes this institution to be more efficient, there would be a move to consider. Nevertheless, adopting that system would deny the deliberative nature of this house.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I recall that in 1940 or 1941, when two members of Congress had the same ghost writer, one of them delivered his oration in the morning by filing it and the other, Fiorel-lo la Guardia, that tribune of the people, rose that afternoon and delivered his in person. The next day they were both amazed to find they had used the same speech. Let us try to elevate this institution by debating, by expressing our views without the necessity of having everything written out, because if it is all written out, and all to be read, a lot of time could be saved.
Then again, we would have a far better attendance in this house if the institution were cut in two. This place is too large. Everybody has a seat. One of my deep regrets is that I did not secure the consent of the house-and I think it could have been obtained at the time-to remove these desks and reduce the size of the chamber so that there would only be seating for 200. In those circumstances hon. members would all be here. Whenever there is a matter of importance to be debated in Westminster, everybody gets there early. I am referring to the membership of the house.
The next thing I want to deal with is that too many members and too many people have the idea that in this institution we make decisions, that we have real powers of government. We have not. I do not go as far as the Prime Minister went in February last when the rules of parliament were thrown out of the window after the defeat of the government in the house. He was minister of justice then. The prime minister and he indicated then that the government was the master of the house. That is a very bad concept indeed. It is true the government has the responsibility of legislation. It must assume that responsibility. We have the right to examine. The great danger of some of the ideas advanced by powerful governments is that in the interest of so-called efficiency private members of the house will apply to themselves the throttle of secrecy which was recently applied by the Prime Minister to members of the government. They have been strong, silent men ever since. At least, they have been silent.

When the Prime Minister said he did not want "leaks," he was right. What takes place in cabinet should not become available to any of us outside that institution. But, sir, today ministers go around almost as though they had tape over their lips lest they speak. We had an example of this today.

A question was asked by the Leader of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition regarding something which happened a few months ago, in January. According to the press, some individual in the civil service had been engaged in one of the most dangerous activities that anyone can engage in as far as his own country is concerned-bartering information to a potential enemy. Maybe today the days of espionage are over. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) brought off a good quip on the subject yesterday. As a matter of fact, the days of espionage are pretty well over because the air is full of marching battalions of those things that move overhead. Now, everybody knows everything about everybody else. But this man would have belonged to that group of people who desire to maintain their anonymity, had it not been for the press.
I realize, as I said today in the course of my question, that on the shoulders of the Prime Minister rests the security of the nation. But parliament has the right, within the limitations imposed by the need for security, to know who this person is. The answer to that question was apparently that he was not as guilty as he thought he was. However, he was kept on for several months and now he belongs to the great unwashed outside the civil service. Who was this person? Is there any reason Canadians should not be told? Whatever he did was detrimental to the state or he would not have been put into general circulation outside the civil service.
This is what is happening today whenever we raise such questions. Those strong, silent men of the government are declining to furnish answers to members of this house. When questions are asked from this side we are given answers one would expect from quiz kids-smart, evasive, diffuse. Let us have the facts. But people over there are apparently not satisfied with the rules as they are today. They want, apparently, to apply to parliament generally the throttle of silence which denies members of the cabinet the right to express themselves except with permission.
IMr. Diefenbaker.]

Change the rules with changing conditions? I accept that. But what happened last February when the rules and the constitutional rights of our country were thrown overboard induces me, usually unsuspecting, to examine very closely what the President of the Privy Council has in mind.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
They talk about examination of the estimates. I do not want to say that anything we do is a joke. The time was fixed for examination of estimates, so many days, 30 days. Liberal members spoke, as they had a right to do. Finally, in the last hours we passed over $1,300 million, just like that, because the time had been used up. Mr. Speaker, as the rules are today the government could put $40 million or $50 million in the estimates and get away with it by holding off discussion until the last hours of the last day. That is not conducive to the discharge of our responsibilities.

I like to hear the President of the Privy Council, in towering majesty, as he stands and speaks of parliament. As I understood him today, and I am only too glad to be corrected, he is concerned over the fact that we take too long to discuss things. Let us clear away that canard as against this parliament and several parliaments.
I am not going to read the record. I sent out for it, and for benefit of the members generally I suggest they should look at Hansard for May 25, 1965, where Hon. Gordon Churchill, who was referred to today by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, analysed this idea that we waste time.
I am not going to repeat the figures that he gave. They are to be found at page 1643. They have now been brought up to date and it is interesting to note the result for the session 1966-67, which commenced on January 18, 1966, and ended May 8, 1967, the longest session in Canadian history. Mention was made by the President of the Privy Council that the tendency today is to have long sessions. Well, until the session I have
September 24, 1968

just referred to, the longest as I recall it was 1904.
The greatest number of bills in a session was passed in 1966-67. That session lasted for 250 sitting days, or almost a year and a half. Some 83 bills were enacted. Of that number 16 were passed with less than 30 minutes debate for each bill. Ten other bills were passed with debate on each one not exceeding one hour. Nine more required less than one and a half hours for consideration. Three others took less than two hours. In other words, of the 83 bills 38 were passed with less than two hours debate for each bill.
Who is there here who will say that record indicates an attitude on the part of the opposition, that they have been engaged in delaying? Eight other bills required over two hours but less than three. Five bills required over three hours but less than four hours for all stages. A total of 51 bills, or 60 per cent of the entire legislative program, were completed in a total of 66 hours, or an average of one hour and 18 minutes per bill. They say we hold them up? Are we to have applied to us that throttle of silence which the members of the administration have today? I thought, Mr. Speaker, that this should go on the record.
The remaining 32 bills took longer. There were two or three that challenged the concepts of the opposition, and we stood and debated them.
Mention was made today that with regard to this omnibus bill that has everything from homosexuality to free love and firearms in it, amendments to the Criminal Code all thrown together in a hodgepodge, this institution would be holding up debate if we were to stand against it because we are opposed to homosexuality, legalized abortion, and a few others of those fancy offences under the law. Let the government divide this bill. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) said only recently that he believed it should be divided. That was before.

But he is on a task force appointed by the Prime Minister, he, a former director of the C.P.R., to bring in a recommendation as to whether or not Air Canada and C.P. Airlines are to be joined together in unholy matrimony. Sir, I admire his judicial temperament because on June 10, speaking in the city of Winnipeg he said this-I do not have the quote here but I know what he said. He said he was in favour of C.P. Sir, to me it is ominous that out of the declarations of a task force, with a chairman who has already expressed what he thinks, there should come recommendations to parliament as to what it should do.
I do not want to speak beyond the dinner hour. I shall summarize. This house cannot be satisfied with the kind of dilly-dally answers that it is receiving from this governement.

You are playing with parliament. It is not your puppet, it is not your plaything. When that course is followed we have a situation where ministers-I imagine they obtain permission first-rush out when they know something cannot be debated in the house and tell the country what they are thinking and what courses ought to be followed. Consideration of Procedural Changes There are one or two other matters which I wish to mention. What about sittings? We could sit longer hours. I believe we sit for a matter of 25 J hours a week. I do not believe in sitting between the hours of six and eight o'clock in the evening. However, while we sit for 251 hours a week, in the British House of Commons they sit for 31 hours a week. There is no reason for our sittings not being extended.
Next, I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that we should have periodic adjournments. It is wonderful to get away from Ottawa, to get away from this vacuum and go out among the people to find out what they are thinking. Thank you. I shall not transgress for very long.
I should like to refer to you, sir. I endeavoured to bring about for this institution a Speaker removed from the controversies of public life. I realize there are two sides to this question but I believe the idea that you should have a constituency in Ottawa, attractive as this area is, where you would sit is contrary to the position you occupy. You are the first commoner; you must be a member of the House of Commons. You would not be if you were chosen as a kind of factotum, having once become Speaker from a constituency.
This will take a long while, I believe, even with the constitutional experts getting together to bring about the making of your position permanent, but I have a suggestion to make. You are impartial and I feel one of the first steps the house should take-I hope I am not contravening in any way the rules of the house-is to provide an additional salary for Mr. Speaker over and above that of today which would be, as in the United Kingdom, free from all deductions and taxes. As well, I believe there should be an official residence for the Speaker of the House of Commons of Canada. In removing yourself from the forum of debate you make a tremendous sacrifice.

DEBATES	September 24, 1968
Therefore I hope this is one step that will appeal to hon. members.
Although I have changed my view in this regard over the years, I think we ought to let the people know what we are doing. To that end the press often condemns us for dilatoriness, inattention, lack of diligence and the like. I think of these young members who come to the house to make their maiden speeches. I try to be here to listen to them. When a new member has something to say and has worked on a speech it is most discouraging when he finds there is no reference to his speech in the press the next day. It is more; it is discomfiting. In the United Kingdom the practice is followed whereby the press reports that "A.B." spoke, with the inclusion of a line or two, and that "B.C." spoke, with the inclusion of a line or two. The importance of members who are trying to find their legislative feet in this institution would be materially increased if the press would give them mention.

maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER PROCEDURAL CHANGES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER PROCEDURAL CHANGES
speechtext:
I should like to see television in this chamber. As I have said, I have changed my mind in this regard over the years. I think much can be done to bring parliament to the people. I believe arrangements could be made between the house leaders whereby, as a beginning, half an hour a day would be made available for this purpose. Someone might say that the people will not watch, that they are more interested in all the horrors and other things that are shown on television. However, they would learn something of this wonderful institution.
In my last words I should like to say that we get so close together that we know each other and we know each other's weaknesses. We also learn to admire those who sit opposite who stand sincerely for principle. I have not yet had the opportunity to pay my tribute to Right Hon. L. B. Pearson. We are often pictured as two great opponents. One would almost think that we were covered with the lather of personal antagonism. As a matter of fact most people do not realize the close relationship that prevails.
These are my ideas of parliament. I hope that this committee when it meets will be sure that it does not diminish the power, the responsibility and the authority of the backbencher. Changes can be made, but those changes should not have the effect of doing what so many powerful governments, whatever their political party, have tried to do to
September 24, 1968

stifle the opposition. The rules must protect primarily the rights of the opposition and above all the rights of private members in this chamber.

the second reading of Bill No. C-101, respecting London and Midland General Insurance Company.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-101 is a bill to change the name of London and Midland General Insurance Company to Avco General Insurance Company. The sole purpose of this bill is to change the name of the company. There are two reasons for the company requiring a change of name. The company is part of the Avco group of companies; the Avco Corporation is the parent company. Last year there was in the United Kingdom a company that used "London and Midland" as the main words in its name. That company went into bankruptcy, and questions have been asked as a result. The company named in this bill received several inquiries as to whether they had any connection with the
Private Bill
United Kingdom, London and Midland company. There is no connection between them whatsoever. That, Mr. Speaker, is one reason for requesting a change of name to Avco General Insurance Company.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
I should like to point out to hon. members that the parent company is Delta Acceptance Corporation, which is the wholly owned subsidiary of Avco Delta Corporation, Delaware, U.S.A. There is one other reason for this company requesting a change of name. I believe there are in Canada ten insurance companies which use the word "London" as part of their corporate name. In an effort to achieve some form of distinctiveness, the company wishes to change its name to Avco General Insurance Company.

maintopic: PRIVATE BILL

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of questions I should like to ask in connection with this bill. The first is, how did it become numbered 101? This is the first private members bill, and I would have thought it should have been numbered 1 rather than 101. This bill was before us on a previous occasion and there has been considerable discussion about the reasons for requesting the change of name. We are happy to have a report from the sponsor of the bill.
There has also been discussion as to whether Avco now owns this company, which was originally under other ownership, and whether the whole Avco complex is part of the Delta Corporation. For this reason I believe the bill should be sent to committee where members will have an opportunity to ask questions of representatives of the company to ascertain whether or not the bill should be passed.
This bill, with a number of others, raises the fairly fundamental proposition of whether we are interested in the proliferation of insurance companies, and second whether this proliferation is in the interest of the shareholders or in the national interest in so far as the expenditure of assets in the mortgage and other lending fields is concerned.
We find in this company, as in many insurance companies which have appeared before us, a similarity in that they are concerned in exactly the same field, but with a slightly different name. Companies owned by a parent company in another country do not fall under the same restrictions as those that are Canadian owned, in that there is in effect no possibility of those Canadians who invest in

Private Bill
the company having a say in how the corporation is run.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I believe an important question is whether it is to the advantage of Canada to incorporate companies such as this. The question of ownership in a foreign country, in a field as important as insurance in this country, will have to be examined. I also believe the superintendent of insurance should be questioned very carefully on his views respecting this matter.
It seems to me this is a matter in which the government should take some interest. I think it is time this whole question was decided. Bills in this form have been introduced in the past few years and we have dealt with 15 or 20 insurance companies that wished to become established, or 15 or 20 companies wanting a change of name or other changes through the parliamentary process. The government should study this question to see whether a proliferation of companies such as this is advantageous to, and in the interest of, the Canadian public.
The fact that these bills go before the private and miscellaneous bills committee does not in itself provide protection for the general public. I think the time has arrived when the government should consider this whole question. If the charges we have been making for the past four or five years with respect to the number of these companies are correct, something should be done about them. If they are incorrect, the committee will be able to ascertain the truth of the matter and arrive at a conclusion.
Many of the companies presenting bills to us in this form, requesting a simple change of name, are really seeking permission to transfer the assets of one corporation to those of another. In some cases these assets are transferred to a very large corporation that is a holding company. All this is outside the sphere of parliament.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the length of the bill and the limited amount of information contained in it are not reasons for hon. members passing the bill at this time. I, therefore, hope that the committee to which the bill is referred will consider the propositions put forward by members in the last four or five years with regard to private members' bills. I hope the committee will look carefully into an alternative method of allowing such companies to be incorporated, to change their names or to make changes in their structure. Such changes have been made through private members' bills.

Hon. members may be aware that a year or two ago the committee did discuss the subject in a general way, and as a result most of those matters concerned with changes of name are no longer dealt with in the house. These changes were put into officialdom by letters patent. If the house leader is really interested in making a useful change, he should look into the question and decide how we should deal with private members' bills such as these. In my opinion some abuse has taken place in the house in the past when general changes were requested instead of the specific changes required. A much better method could be devised than the one in operation at the moment.
We know that committees will soon be set up. I hope this bill will soon be sent to the committee in order that it may examine the whole procedure of private members' bills. These bills are sponsored by private members who often have no knowledge of and no control over the matter. Private members have only the information supplied to them. They are Joe'd to do the job and often suffer abuse for no good reason. In many cases, the bill he introduces does not affect him or his riding. I believe this procedure leaves us open to abuse and a better system should be devised for handling these bills. As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I hope the committee will consider this whole question in the time it has before other, similar bills appear on our order paper.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the very great pleasure tonight of congratulating you on two counts. I congratulate you on your re-election to the office of Speaker of the House of Commons, which is a position you have earned as a result of your conduct during the last several sessions. I also congratulate you on the second count, one of which few may be aware, and certainly one that very few mention. It will be recalled that during the past six years I have made several comments about the situation in which the page boys find themselves. On occasion I have condemned this institution for assisting these young lads to become drop-outs from school. In the past I have made representations to at least three other Speakers, and finally to you, Mr. Speaker.
It is to your credit, sir, that you have taken cognizance of the situation, and I should like to point out to hon. members that there is a different arrangement now in respect of page boys. I understand they are over 16 years of age and are not drop-outs from school. It is to your credit, sir, that something has been done about this situation, and I should like to congratulate you on this action. It indicates a feeling on your part for even the smallest group, and I know that you will continue to show an interest in these young lads. This will result in their being able to go on to even greater things in the House of Commons.
The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) has placed several propositions before this house and I should first like to comment on the reforms as set out by him. The right hon. gentleman, the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), has reminded us that this house has no other purpose than to protect and preserve freedom. I agree that this is one of the main functions of this house. There is another function that the public expects us to perform, and that is to get things done.

Consideration of Procedural Changes
The minister gave the members a brief history of parliament, but I suggest he did not go far enough. Parliament, in essence, originated as a group of commoners called together to express their grievances. Originally the Crown chose its ministers and its governors, and when taxes were required parliament was called. Each member came to express the grievances of the residents of particular parts of the United Kingdom. They would suggest that things were wrong in their constituencies or localities. One such gentleman probably suggested that the Sheriff of Nottingham was a very bad fellow.
After expressing their grievances these representatives voted the requested money and went home. To this day there has been little change, except the ministers are not appointed now by the Crown but by the Prime Minister. In fact, this house still has that main function of expressing grievances. There is little communication between the backbenchers on either side of the house with those who occupy the seats of the mighty. This is an acknowledged fact.
I have my doubts as to the mightiness of those who sit in these seats, except those who sit as politicians. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in a recent speech felt it necessary to warn his ministers that he expects them to set policy from now on rather than the administrators. Anything we can do to bring more power to the backbenchers on both sides of this house will be of benefit to parliament.
The right hon. gentleman cannot argue that originally there were two parties in the House of Commons. Originally, all the members of the commons opposed the Crown. It was not until recently that the party system evolved. The right hon. gentlemen opposite and backbenchers come here and have a field day and, with the exception of the odd individual on this side, there seems to be very little purpose in their being here.

speechtext:
It is not surprising that Canadians as a whole have lost a great deal of ropect for parliament and members of this house. We now have the opportunity of doing something about this. The parliamentary system is really not suited to an economy which changes as quickly as the Canadian economy has changed during the past 20 or 30 years. This is a wonderful institution which would probably work well in a static or agrarian

economy. It has worked in the United Kingdom, but it is not even working very well there today. When you have an economy such as ours, which changes from a static position to a very fast-moving position, messages from constituents have to be conveyed to the government immediately. One cannot afford to wait very long for the administrators to decide that an idea proposed on behalf of a constituent is a good one. The people expect us to do things, yet we have to inform them that we have no power.
On several occasions the minister mentioned Westminster. I hope he was not suggesting that we should follow or ape the actions of those at Westminster. Many of the reforms in the House of Commons in England have been good, and I think we should consider them, but this is not England. We are faced with areas with problems that are vastly different from those in existence there. We have a different economy and different requirements. Indeed, I have no hesitation in saying that Canada is much more suited to a republican system than a parliamentary system. I hold no brief for the republican system, but elements of republicanism could be worked into a parliamentary system.
I think there is an advantage in not having as much control over the money as we have under our system. That is the case in a republican system.
Let me explain what I hope will happen to our committees as a result of the proposed changes. Specifically, let me refer to what the minister has said about the referral of estimates to these committees. Before I do so let me suggest that there is a presumption that all new members come here to learn a new trade or new profession. This is not to say, Mr. Speaker, that we were sent to parliament by our constituents because we were the most able people in the riding. The backbenchers were not sent here to learn some new business for their own self-aggrandizement or promotion.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)

I would say that most backbenchers have quite a bit of knowledge. Indeed, some of us who have been here for six years, all fired up with new ideas when we came, have lost sight of the trees because of the branches. After a while you get confused. In fact, Mr. Speaker, new members are told to
September 24, 1968

settle down, that they will learn about parliament in five or six years. I say they are better members now than they will be six years from now.
Under the old committee system, Mr. Speaker, a member could work very hard. He could research and he could question. But by and large, committee reports came back to the house, were filed or tabled, and no one saw them again. After five or six years, sometimes sooner, members would wonder why they had done all that work. You might as well have been playing tic-tac-toe.
As the minister explained, the administration, through the minister, finds out how much money is needed for each department for the following year. These estimates then come to the house in the blue book, and during consideration of estimates you can argue about anything so long as it has some relationship to a particular item. I remember the former member for Port Arthur used to stand up and move the reduction of an item in the estimates from, say, $75 million or $100 million to $1, and this constituted a vote of confidence.
The administration in those days, Mr. Speaker, had an absolutely free hand. They were never questioned. Nobody ever wondered what item 7, say, was all about, or where some $47,000 was going, because he didn't have time. Besides, it did not matter because you either voted for $1 or for $75 million or $100 million.
If the minister said what I thought he said, Mr. Speaker, that from now on the estimates of each department will go to a parliamentary committee, then this means that we backbenchers will have a lot of time to examine and to question the administration. If backbenchers feel that something is not quite right with a certain department, then they can make things rather miserable for the administrator. Indeed, there will be nothing particularly wrong, if you feel sufficiently strongly about a matter, to move a reduction in the amount of the estimates.
This might be one of the recommendations in the report, and I am sure that the backbenchers who sit on my side of the house will find lots of help from hon. members opposite. If a member feels that his constituents want him to do so, in the report he can recommend a reduction in the amount of the estimates concerned and the minister will consequently be embarrassed. When the report is presented to the house the question can be raised again. There is at least some indication 29180-281
Consideration of Procedural Changes that there is objection to some aspect of the administration and that you have been able to voice that objection.
Believe me, Mr. Speaker, I feel that from now on the power of the backbencher and the power of this House of Commons is going to be greater, not less. I believe most members will act responsibly. I am sure there will come a time when members, even on the government side, will not agree with a particular item of the estimates of a department and they will have the right to make their objections known. This will not constitute a vote of confidence. Hon. members will not be expected to vote the government down, thereby throwing us into another election campaign.
What I have said, Mr. Speaker, may be regarded as what I call a caricature of government. I am sure the right hon. gentleman and other hon. members opposite, as well as those on this side who have been ministers will agree that it is a caricature. But by and large, Mr. Speaker, it is a fairly composite picture. Ideas and policy decisions do not necessarily stem from the ministers because they are busy politicians. However, as Professor Porter pointed out, we do have a very large establishment in Ottawa composed of people of great consequence, the elite with family histories going back two or three hundred years and who all belong to the right clubs.
Occasionally, these people get the message across that it would be a good idea if the government instituted a certain measure. The department and deputy minister concerned immediately think it is a wonderful idea. The next thing you know, a resolution appears, followed by a bill which is practically word for word what is wanted. The minister and cabinet go over it, but the first time we see the bill is when it appears on the order paper.
Then, consider the administrator or deputy minister who wants $600 million for his department. He says to himself that he may have an emergency during the coming year so had better put in for $670 million. However, treasury board will cut that by 15 per cent so he adds on 15 per cent, though I doubt whether in the end the money is reduced. If the department has not spent that money near the end of the fiscal year, then they had better spend it quickly or they will not get any more.
At what stage, Mr. Speaker, do we as parliamentarians enter the picture during the passage of a bill? I heartily endorse the
September 24, 1968

Consideration of Procedural Changes minister's stand because I think it will give backbenchers and all members of parliament an opportunity to question, argue with and talk to the administration. The administration will listen to all your complaints and do things for you, which I think is all to the good. I know, and I am sure the Prime Minister knows, that each minister will trust that all of us on this side will support the government, unless there is some matter of serious consequence. In that case, the minister will realize that something does displease certain constituents and there will be quick communication.
The Prime Minister has said that there must be communication from all Canadians. At the moment it is a one-way street; the government can communicate with the public, but it is very difficult to get any communication from the public to the government. As a result, Mr. Speaker, we have task forces. The president of the Liberal federation comes up with a very good idea in an attempt to involve the people. There is no better way to involve the people than through members of parliament; after all, that is what we are here for. But there is no sense in being involved and making representations if one knows one will not be listened to or that no one will care. However, if you control the purse then people will care.
I am heartily in favour of amendment of the rules. I hope this resolution is approved by everyone in the house. I do not think it will diminish the power of the opposition, the power of the backbencher or even the power of the front bench. It will enhance our prestige, our power and make us aware of our responsibilities.

Mr. Speaker, I had little difficulty in deciding to participate in this debate, because it is a well known fact that, besides being interested in the examination of the rules, I have followed their development very closely.
As I was, six years ago, discharging the duties that that you are now so honourably and brilliantly performing, and because of my experience as a member of several committees on house procedure, I would like at this time to record certain remarks in Hansard.

First of all, Mr. Speaker, may I say I listened with some degree of amusement yesterday to two rather-if the hon. gentlemen will forgive me for using the term-intemperate


speeches wherein the house was castigated for having wasted time up to now. These members indicated that they thought the throne speech was irrelevant. Over the years, I have heard a few of those speeches and all I can say is that members who delivered that type of speech were distinguished by one characteristic; they were one timers who seemed to work their frustrations out to the point where they missed being elected the next time around. I think when some hon. members have a little more experience they will concede that some of their remarks were better left unsaid.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
The question of the reform of parliament and the rules of parliament has been bothering people for some time. Their zeal for reform is like a spring cold that turns into year round sniffles. I suppose that when editorial writers are short of copy they can always write something about the reform of parliament. It seems to be a popular subject on the hustings during election campaigns. I heard some candidates who knew not where the front door of this place was say that parliament had to be reformed and that they would come down here, cut a wide swath through the thicket, and this house would soon be in order.
Well, it seems to me that the greatest noise about the reform of parliament and its procedures is made by those who have little or no knowledge of what happens here and how it happens. In any event, we have heard a great deal about the reform of parliament. Some changes have been made over the years. There has been an evolution.
May I point out to hon. members, and this has been pointed out by the right hon. gentleman for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) and others, that every time there has been a major change in the rules it has been at the expense of the membership of the house and in favour of the executive. This so called passion for efficiency has always been exercised at the expense of this institution. Parliament is not a board of directors. It is not an administrative body, nor is it merely a rubberstamp for the omniscience that has suddenly descended on 20 or 25 men who are aided by administrators.

supporting the administration the backbencher on the government side has about "zot" to say about policy and the formulation of statutes. He sees what is contained in a bill after the bill has been printed. That is how he learns what is in a government bill.
There has been agitation, and we hope it will meet with success for private members to become involved in legislation at an earlier stage than the stage of, shall we say, getting into the brambles and clearing out the brambles in the clause by clause study in the committee stage after second reading.
There are some comments I wish to make about the general subject of legislation. This afternoon I heard the views of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald). I think, myself, that the provisional rule with regard to the resolution stage being limited to about a five hour debate is commendable. That rule has worked out reasonably well. It may need a somewhat longer trial, but I think it will work. With the greatest respect, Mr. Speaker, I think we should be better off during any debate on any resolution stage if those who prepare the speeches or statements of the minister adhered to the rule of relevancy. For instance, if we are to deal with some measure of social significance we do not need to hear the record of the past generation regarding the performance of the administration in the field of social welfare. If that is put on the record everybody else is entitled to comment; the debate becomes wide open, and that is quite wrong. Our first reform might be to prevent discussion on a bill from becoming irrelevant. Mind you, where that has happened it has not necessarily been through any fault of the Chair.
If hon. members turn to page 562 of Hansard for 1962, they will see that on that occasion I spoke at some length about the question period and the role of the Speaker in the enforcement of rules in the house. One can see that the responsibility for upholding the rules rests as much on the members of the house as on the Chair. We may compare our rules to the rules governing any football or hockey game. Not only must the officials overseeing the game know and observe the rules, but the players must also know and observe the rules; otherwise, the game becomes a shambles. Similarly, the proceedings in this house could become a shambles.
With regard to first reading, there is a suggestion to send a bill, after we have first seen it, to a committee, unless the house decides otherwise. There are many minor

Consideration of Procedural Changes bills which it would be nonsense to send to committee. In these instances, the house could agree not to send them to committee. We could then go from first reading or to second reading without sending the bill to committee.
It seems to me that in this matter we could adopt the practice, not of the British parliament, but of European parliaments where legislation after being printed goes to an appropriate committee. The committee could then work out any amendments it wished. Committee members are free to move amendments to legislation without being committed a fortiori by their vote. It is nonsense for government members to suggest a worthwhile amendment to a bill which is in some sense contrary to a proposal of the government if they are already committed by a vote on second reading in favour of the bill. In that case the government members would stand up and say, "Aye" all the way along.
I suggest, therefore, that it is of greater advantage to permit committee members to be free to make such amendments as they wish to make, with the proviso that when the bill is reported back the government has the right to accept or reject any amendments. If the bill has been thoroughly gutted in committee the government can say, "Vote on the report of the committee, and the vote shall be one of confidence." This is a point where I think the government ought to have an option of asking for confidence.
I put that suggestion forward for the consideration of hon. members. If it were adopted it seems to me that we should eliminate much repetitious debate on second reading, since the second reading debate would take place on the reporting back of the bill. The bill would be debated on principle of the acceptance of the report and the clauses to be considered in detail, and off it would go. It seems to me that that would give a much better chance for a working committee dealing with the legislative side to do its work.
I could not possibly cover all I want to say this evening. I could spend half an hour alone on the subject of the question period, which I will not leave entirely alone since I must say this: I have noticed that whenever a maximum time was fixed for any question period or period for debate in this house, that has immediately become a minimum time. In the past, with direction from the Chair and cooperation from members, the question period was often cut down to 10, 15 or 20 minutes. Perhaps with the shortening of questions and a greater use of the order paper the question period could again be shortened.

By agreement there has been a suspension of Standing Order 15A, one of the most pernicious rules we had. Thank goodness, it is in suspension. It actually was some sort of half-hearted borrowing of an idea from the business committee of the British parliament. If one wants to see the mess the British committee system is in and the sort of practice that became prevalent at Westminster, one need only read British Hansard for May 23, 1965, a celebrated occasion when Dame Irene Ward, a senior and delightful member of the British house, was suspended for five days because she protested so vehemently that Mr. Speaker had to eject her. Why? Because she objected to the finance bill which was the subject of an order by the business committee. The schedule set was a fantastic one. I can say from personal experience that back in 1948 when the House of Commons was considering the nationalization of steel, the nationalization of transport, the national health bill and a number of other major bills under the Labour government, scores and scores of important clauses were never touched under the rigid time-table set out by the business committee. This despite the fact that the government itself had amendments to introduce to a number of these clauses. Last May the same thing happened again in connection with the transport bill. The measures then have to go to the House of Lords; that body is overloaded with the amendments, some of which are accepted and others refused. Then the bill has to go back to the commons for consultation and the working out of an agreed version as between the two chambers. This is an unwieldy process, yet it is supposed to be the epitome of efficiency. Why? Because there is a time-table for the benefit of the cabinet. I have talked

DEBATES	September 24, 1968
with any number of members on both sides who are beside themselves with sheer frustration at being unable to speak at any time on such important bills.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
When, for instance, the British white paper on defence was up for discussion last year it was my recollection, subject to correction, that in the time allocated prior to the closing of the house at 10.30 fewer than 12 members out of 600 were able to speak on such an important subject as defence policy. Not only Conservative members but Labour members were indignant because they could not speak even for one minute. The minister of defence took an hour himself to open the discussion, and seized a good deal of time at the end to close the debate. I would therefore caution hon. members against the idea that our problems with the rules will be cured by the establishment of a business committee and the allocation of time through a cut and dried schedule. We are only heading for more trouble that way.
One of the things I might suggest is that speeches, apart from those made by a minister who is proposing legislation or by someone who is following a text closely for the purpose, say, of adducing statistics, should not be read. After all, members were elected to the House of Commons and they did not gain the backing of the voters by standing before them and reading a prepared text.

May I draw attention to an item which appeared in the Times of London in connection with the expulsion of Dame Irene Ward? This is an extract taken from the Canadian Bar Journal of August, 1968. I read as follows:
When Dame Irene Ward clashed with the Speaker and was suspended from the House, she dramatically brought to public attention the plight of members which had been expressed by the parliamentary correspondent of The Times thus:
"The Palace of Westminster was seething with unrest today, with M.P.'s chasing around like angry ants that have suddenly had their comfortable hill broken open and scattered. Anguish and frustration knew no bounds as 15 committees considering bills and other matters competed with the debate on the floor of the House on the transport bill, which began the second day of its three day marathon at 10 a.m.
Every time there was a division on the transport bill, proceedings in committees had to be halted so that members could rush to the division lobbies. M.P.'s ancient and modern were being hauled up and down stairs like a regiment of protesting yo-yos. Committee after committee fumed and fussed under the pressure.'*
Lord Dalkeith, (Conservative M.P., North Edinburgh) was caught on the timing of events when he discovered he could not cover 2 committees and his duties in the House and as a result missed a division on the Social Work (Scotland) bill. He had banged and thumped on the door to the committee room but it was locked for the discussion. His entry, after the vote was counted, was greeted by laughter and cheers but he was furious in his protests.
The whole House runs the risk of being worked to a breakdown as the machine tries to digest the number of bills being considered. One day there were three committees in the morning and five in the afternoon and the House in session. Dame Irene Ward (Conservative M.P., Tynemouth) wrote to The Times and warned that the sending of important legislation to committee and the chaotic conditions caused by so many committees was starting Britain "on the road to a Social dictatorship". She said in the letter: "The British public should examine with great care the parliamentary happenings of today".
Mr. Speaker, this, in essence, is the justification for the warning I give with regard to thinking that mere reform of rules in whatever fashion hon. members in their wisdom may see fit will necessarily be the cure-all for all that happens here.
There is another sector to which I wish to advert, and that is the private members' hour. I think this house owes a responsibility to proposers of this legislation, and somehow or other we must find a way by which legitimate debate can take place on the bills put forward. Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the resolution, but since this is my first opportunity to speak on the floor of this house I would like at the outset to say a few words of tribute to my very distinguished predecessor. I have the honour to represent the new riding of Windsor-Walkerville, which is the successor riding of the old constituency of Essex East. That electoral district will be linked for all time with the name of the member who represented it from 1935 until April of this year. He was successively Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour, Secretary of State, Minister of Health and Welfare and, after a period in vigorous opposition, Secretary of State for External Affairs. He is now Government Leader in the other chamber. By common acknowledgement, he is one of the great parliamentarians in Canada's political history, and it is fitting that the name of the riding which he so magnificently represented for 33 years should be retired from this house with him. It is both a privilege and a challenge to succeed so great a Canadian, and it is a source of special satisfaction that he has
428	COMMONS
Consideration of Procedural Changes assumed the designation in the other chamber of the Senator from Windsor-Walkerville.
On another occasion, Mr. Speaker, I hope to speak about my riding and its concerns, unemployment, insufficient housing, poverty and pollution. However, tonight I must confine myself to the resolution at hand. Legislatures, as institutions of representative government, are today confronted with the most serious intellectual challenge they have ever faced. The seriousness of the challenge results from the fact that it arises from within democratic theory rather than as previously from outside, from totalitarian or absolutist dogmas which of their very nature were challenges of force, not intellect. The internal challenge is that raised by the proponents of what is called participatory democracy.
There are many aspects of the movement of participatory democracy that we all applaud. To the extent that it means the active interest of all citizens in matters political and a very full participation by them in political parties and movements, with a corresponding openness of the political process to popular participation, it is only the perfection of the present system of representative government.
This may indeed be all that it means to many of its adherents. But to its theoreticians it means the abolition of representative government as insufficiently responsive to the needs of the people, especially to those of the dispossessed, and its replacement by a system of direct democracy in which every decision is made collectively by the whole population. Perhaps in a technologically more advanced age in which information and opinion on every issue could be conveyed directly and instantaneously to each citizen, with an equally direct and instantaneous return by the citizen to a central source, a nonrepresentational democracy would be feasible. But in the meantime it would be tantamount either to mob rule or to an oligarchy.
Often, however, an evil is merely the exaggeration of a good, and the development of a fallacious theory may serve the purpose of calling our attention to inadequacies in our present practice. Hopefully, the movement toward participatory democracy will direct our minds towards the achievement of more democratic representational government, characterized by greater openness and by more opportunities for meaningful participation in decision making. In my opinion, such democratization is needed in our governmental operations and, I might add, in all our political parties.
[Mr. MacGuigan.l

I would therefore suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the primary principle of parliamentary reform should be the principle of democracy, by which I mean in this context an opportunity for more meaningful and more widespread participation in law making. I believe that this principle would have as its consequence more adequate law making; I do not mean more efficient since efficiency could be taken to mean merely the quantity of achievement in a given time whereas what I have in mind is a more qualitative test of effective operation. More adequate law making means the creation of legislation which is more attuned to the social problems of the day, which will be better received by the public, and which will be of more lasting benefit to the country.
From this starting point, it would appear that the thrust of parliamentary reform should be directed in considerable part toward the creation of a system of permanent standing committees, with greatly expanded powers, as the most effective means of increasing participation in law making. At first glance the referring of legislation from the whole house to a committee of, say, 20 members may not appear to increase participation, at least quantitatively. But in truth it would not only expand participation qualitatively, by allowing for a much fuller participation in law making by the committee members than would be possible for any members of parliament in the committee of the whole, but it would achieve this gain without diminishing the rights of any other members of this house to participate in plenary session. Moreover, while the principal benefit with respect to the operation of any particular committee would be qualitative, the total picture of the operation of the committee system would show an immense overall quantitative gain by the collectivity of members in real law making.
I would therefore, Mr. Speaker, express the following hopes with respect to the committee's recommendations:
1.	That it would recommend a system of permanent standing committees which would operate for the complete life of a parliament. Normally, the same members would be members of these committees from session to session, and the committees would have power to sit while parliament was not in session and, indeed, might use that time extensively.
2.	That each standing committee would have a permanent jurisdiction over a particular class of legislation. All bills and resolutions would be referred to the standing
September 24, 1968	COMMONS
committee having jurisdiction over the predominant subject matter. If the jurisdiction of the various committees were defined sufficiently precisely, the decision on allocation would normally be a routine one, although occasionally a jurisdictional decision might have to be made by the house.
3.	That while a standing committee would remain a creature of the house and would be bound to deal with matters referred to it by the house, it would also have independent power to investigate matters falling within its jurisdiction, subject of course to approval by the house of its operating budget. I would be inclined to the view that every standing committee should have a minimum annual budget, with supplementary appropriations made at the house's discretion for special assignments.
4.	That a permanent staff of experts, translators and secretaries would be assigned to each standing committee. On the premise of a stable division of legislative responsibility among committees, the staff could usefully operate on a year round basis.
5.	That bills should be referred to standing committees after first reading in the house. This procedure would give the committees the maximum opportunity to participate collectively in law making, and at the same time would provide the government, which up to that time would have had the advice of only a small circle of experts, with the maximum advantages of committee scrutiny.

It will be obvious, Mr. Speaker, that what I am recommending for the consideration of the special committee is in large measure the structure of the United States congressional committee system. I would hasten to add, however, that we should avoid the great disadvantages of the United States system- the seniority rule for the selection of committee chairmen and members and the power of chairmen or committees to bottle up legislation which they do not like for indefinite periods of time. But I see no danger of such an undue emphasis on committee autonomy in our system. The danger I see is rather that insufficient use might be made of the great talents of the members of all parties in this house, talents which caused them to be selected by the voters of Canada to serve in this august assembly. To the exent that our Canadian democracy is inadequate, let us begin the process of perfecting it with

A further advantage of the committee s ystem I have recommended is that it could perform much of the work assigned in recent years to royal commissions, departmental committees and government task forces. Of course, a place will always remain for such ad hoc bodies to study highly technical matters or perhaps occasionally for matters of considerable political sensitivity. But much of the work that has been done by commissions could have been done just as well by legislative committees. Such a change would eliminate much of the action gap that has occurred between recommendation and legislation, both because the legislative proposals that would be forthcoming would be more politically realistic and because being already under parliamentary consideration they would be somewhat closer to realization. The result would be more adequate law making.
Perhaps as a newly elected member I ought not to have aired my views on parliamentary reform until I had acquired more seasoning in this house. But the times are urgent, and the necessity for parliamentary reform is more urgent still. I, therefore, have presumed to tread disrespectfully upon the hallowed ground of precedent in the cause of reform. I dare to hope that my impetuosity may be regarded in a spirit of charity, even though my proposals must be weighed on the scales of justice.

Mr. Speaker, because these are my first words of debate in this parliament I should like to incorporate all the nice words that have been said about you into my comments tonight. I know that in the future you will be just as fair and impartial as you have been in the past.
I shall not take very long tonight. However, I should like to speak in a practical vein. Through the medium of communications, newspapers, T.V. and radio, there has been a growing demand that parliament must be reformed. I do not think that any one of us would deny that there is some need for reform. We must remember, however, that the rules of parliament, the same as the rules in any other institution, are the tools with which we work. They are simple tools and I believe we must be careful that we do not allow ourselves to be worried too much when we are engaging in this kind of reform by the demands for reform by the press.
September 24, 1968

Consideration of Procedural Changes
At the outset, I wish to say to the minister who moved the resolution that at least he has spelled out some of his thoughts. Politics today has generally caught the imagination. It has become the Madison Avenue instrument today. Men and parties are sold like packaged breakfast food and stainless steel blue blades. So, when we consider reform of the tools of this house we must analyse them very carefully to be sure that we are not brainwashed by the demand for reform in certain places. Otherwise, we might end up curing the evil with worse.
We must remember at the outset that the committee will be like all standing committees of the House of Commons. The committee will be controlled by a majority of government members. I should like to mention my experience so far as committee work of this parliament is concerned. Whether it is a Conservative government or a Liberal government, all committees are controlled by the government. With the exception of the public accounts committee the chairmen of committees generally are appointed from the government side. No doubt we will have the same situation in respect of this committee. The chairmen of the committees know full well what the government wants, and in this case the chairman will know the reforms for which the government is looking.
As one speaker said this afternoon, so far as these instruments and tools are concerned, although they may be of great advantage to the government majority they may be a disadvantage to the opposition. A committee is controlled by the government. The chairman is a member of the government. The government has a majority of the members on a committee. My experience is that witnesses appear before committees, are examined and then a report is prepared. Perhaps I am a little harsh in this regard, but my experience again is that because of the weight of the hon. members on the committee who are controlled by the government, whether it be a Conservative or a Liberal government, that report generally is shaped by the committee chairman and the majority on the committee according to government thinking. Therefore, I do not think we should attend this committee, where we will be outnumbered, in the belief that we will get our ideas across when we point out some of the disadvantages of the suggestions. It might well be that this committee will be operating somewhat in a vacuum.
I should like to use as an illustration the problems in respect of the national parks of

Canada. Leases and lands were being expropriated from the citizens of Jasper and Banff without notice or compensation. So, after pressure from the opposition the government decided to send a committee to that area. I mention this in order to show the weakness of the committee system. If the minister in question or the government can show me how we can reform the committee system, then I will have more faith in it and will have more faith in the ability of the standing committees of the house to examine carefully and properly the estimates of the government. In respect of Banff and Jasper, the committee members went to these parks where briefs were presented. I was told by one of the officials when a certain question came up, that we should be careful of what we say because the government did not like this idea.
In short, the committee was a sham. I do not think any other committees are much better. The committees are no better than some of the administrative boards before which lawyers appear with clients, only to find that a decision has been made before the board is called to order. I want an impartial committee. I want an impartial chairman of the committee. Then, I will have faith that we can go to the committee meetings and come out with a reasonable report which, to some extent, will represent the opinion of the members of the House of Commons rather than merely the opinion of those on the government side of the house. This particular committee to which I refer which visited the national parks was just a kangaroo court, and it came up with a kangaroo decision. It did not solve the problem because the same problem exists today. The people are no more satisfied than they were before.
I think this is where we must start. There are two points. We must place the matter before a committee. Then, we must know whether that committee will be a responsible committee or whether the ideas of the government will be thrust upon it. If that is the case, then it is really going to be just a sham committee. If the estimates are to be more carefully considered by the various standing committees, I suggest that the committees themselves should be so constituted that they will express the viewpoint of the members of the House of Commons and not the viewpoint of one party which constitutes the majority on that committee.

That has been my experience in respect of committees, whether it was the committee on

There is a dangerous aspect to this proposal which I think the committee should consider. I would also point out that the government is very sensitive with regard to certain things. For example, last year our negotiating team in respect of the international wheat agreement failed to reach Geneva on time so they could set a floor price on wheat and guarantee markets to Canada, which markets had been lost because there was a surplus in the United States. We lost some of our traditional markets. We could not debate the question because the government held the matter over to the last hour of our sitting. They can do this so easily. All they have to do is call upon the backbenchers to do the talking on estimates which are not in issue, delay a matter until the last hour and then billions of dollars worth of estimates go through with no debate. This is what happens when the government finds itself in difficulty.
