Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion that has taken place today. The discussion appears not to be a continuation of what was said last year and perhaps even the year before, when we had a minority government and there was a great need for co-operation on both sides of the house. Rather, there has been a return to firm positions that were held somewhere around 1962 when the provisional rules were introduced and which have been in operation off and on ever since.
When the government house leader made his presentation today it was quite obvious that he had the details all worked out and was ready to put them into effect. The debate was a necessity, as many debates are, only because under today's rules we have this type of debate. But the details were already spelled out, and ready to be put into effect.
I have always been very impressed with the house leader of the official opposition, but today I found him not to be progressive in any way, shape or form in his approach to the rules. He has gone back to an ultra-Conservative view that he has not held for a considerable length of time. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I wonder what the exercise is really all about.
It is true that in the last election the general public had something to say about this matter. I was very interested in three of the statements the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made during the election campaign. All of them concerned problems that apparently could be solved almost with a sweep of the hand. One was that we recognize Red China; second that we get out of NATO; and, third that we reform parliament. I think most of the country agreed with these three proposals. I am sure the Prime Minister himself agreed with them and was not just talking 
through his hat. These were very sensible things to do, until he was in a position where he was able to do them. Then, it did not become so simple; other factors entered into the problem.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
With regard to the recognition of Red China, I am sure there were people in other parts of the country who were not so sure this was a good idea. I think probably even Red China may not want to be recognized. When it came to withdrawing from NATO, a situation arose which was obviously not considered at the time the statement was made. However, it is difficult to foresee all the implications. I am sure that the same is true of the proposal to change the rules. It sounded a very easy thing to do during the election. I am sure that all the backbenchers in every part of the house agree with the Prime Minister that we should change the rules to make this a much better place in which to operate and in which to serve the needs of the people of Canada. The difficulty arises when it comes to actually getting down to changing these rules. It is not that we do not want to do something about changing them, but the difficulty is how to change them.
Obviously the rules of parliament were developed over many years by trial and error. This goes back further than my own knowledge of history. However, the development of procedures has taken place under the democratic system which has provided great freedom for the individual and at the same time provided some form of protection to society. I was intrigued by the argument put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) when he said that Mackenzie King, our former prime minister, had decided to allow the throne speech debate to run for 30 days or more during which time he could get on with the business of parliament. I am not sure that I would be opposed to that. I think that a certain number of points would be made by the backbenchers concerning their own constituencies which would give to everyone a better understanding of some of the problems of the day. The issues which were raised by the press could be repeated in the house, and this would be similar to a continuation of the question period conducted throughout the whole day.
However, if an emergency arose, the democratic process could take over and the machinery would still be available to take care of the emergency. I am dubious when we refer
September 24, 1968

to the committee system in the United States which is often mentioned in the house by hon. members whose constituencies lie close to the United States border. There may be some arguments in favour of the system there, but it seems to me we must be very careful in following a system which would prevent us from dealing with emergencies as they arise. Lloyd George and Winston Churchill were mentioned today as statesmen whose contributions were not recognized until the need for them arose. The democratic process has allowed this, and in time of wars or calamities has provided the nation with leadership while preserving the rights of the individual.
I am not suggesting that the rules should not be changed, but I am still a backbencher at heart and will always remain one. Fundamentally, I believe that the rights of the individual are more important than some of our other collective rights. So, I think that if we eliminate the rules which allow the backbencher to have his say when he feels strongly enough on a subject, parliament will become poorer. This is what may happen if we structure the committee system in accordance with that followed by the United States congress. I do not believe this can happen in our parliamentary system. We would have to change to a republican form of government before being able to follow the congressional system. Perhaps there are some who might be prepared to support such a change, but at the moment the house is not faced with this proposition.
There are a number of things which the government should do if they really wish to reform parliament and about which they should inform the house, particularly the new members who are not really aware of what these changes may entail. I am sure many of us will be here for some time without really understanding all the rules. However, if the government is to be fair, it should not present parliament with a fait accompli and then say the majority would accomplish this anyway following a long debate. The government should be prepared to outline how far it intends to go in the changes which it proposes.
One of the things which has to be done I think is for the committee to consider the possibility of a four year term for the government. I have been here 11 years during which time we fought six elections. At least three of these elections were called because the Prime Minister decided it was to his personal advantage to call an election. In my opinion, in

Consideration of Procedural Changes three of these instances he did not consider the interests of the country nor did he consider the members of his party or the opposition. He certainly did not consider the good of the country. I found during the last election that the people in the country were fed up with elections; they have had too many of them. They would like to see members get busy and at least do three years of work before contemplating another election. So, I believe that one of the changes will have to be a four year term for parliament. I suggest that this be done by statute and that the Prime Minister lose the prerogative of calling an election when it suits his fancy. At the same time, I believe we should consider the problems which this would entail in the case of a minority government. I say to the backbenchers on the government side that they should consider the possibility of a minority government being in office in the days to come. The rules should not only apply to the type of government which we have today, but should also be applicable in other cases.
I have a suggestion, therefore, which is contained in a bill, namely that when 15 members approach Mr. Speaker with a resolution to move the dissolution of parliament that motion should be put on the order paper and debated. When a majority of 75 per cent of the members approve this motion, an election be called. It is generally agreed that when members unanimously vote against the government and for a dissolution, the government has really reached the end of the road in any case. Parliament should have the right to make the decision on its dissolution. In any case, I believe this action should not be the prerogative of the Prime Minister. Such a change in the rules would create greater stability in parliament because, as hon. members who have been here in the last two or three parliaments will know, there has been a continuous election campaign during those periods of instability during which an election could have been called at any time, and very little work was done.
The government should also give some consideration to the cost of elections. If they are sincerely interested in reform, they will have to consider the provision of funds which they themselves will designate for the running of elections. In my opinion, this move would eliminate a great deal of competition and the scramble for money which goes on at that time. This will have quite an influence on the man who decides to run.

This may not be the answer to all our problems but I commend him for his initiative in this regard. He has come here without any obligation to any political party. Surely, a Philadelphia lawyer could not tell you what those ten or 15 words on that paper actually mean. They certainly do not convey what is intended. One would be lying if one answered yes or no. The question is similar to that well-known question; have you stopped beating your wife? period, and the Speaker has a responsibility in this regard.

Under certain circumstances, use is made of the guillotine provisions. I am opposed to them, and I think I always shall be. I do admit that certain circumstances are similar to those encountered by negotiators in strike settlements. The time finally arrives when a decision has to be made to settle a strike, but it is often very difficult to get the two sides together. There must be some ultimate method of ending a debate.
We face a danger in adopting changes of the type to which I have referred in that very often there is no balancing protection. In the extreme case there would be no debate, and I am sure the house leader would

His job is to see that we work in this direction, though his own backbenchers may object if they feel he goes too far. They would attend one or two hearings of that committee in this way and accomplish little else than getting their name down. I suggest that the work itself is not important; it is whether some action is taken as a result of that work.
Under the present parliamentary structure committees can, without taking anything away from parliament, go into matters of detail and then report to the house. This report then becomes the subject of debate. Let me give an example, Mr. Speaker. Twice during the course of 10 years I was a member of a farm machinery inquiry committee. Both committees in my opinion did an excellent job. Let us say that they made 10 concrete proposals to the government. Out of these 10 the government agreed with four. However, I felt that having spent all that effort and time listening to farm machinery companies and everybody else concerned, the government damn well should have taken action on those four recommendations.
Let me give another example for the farmers present. We found that fittings that connected the hydraulic system of a machine to the tractor required five or six different types of connectors. This meant that when a farmer bought a new tractor he had to buy a whole new set of adaptors. The committee suggested that there should be a uniform type of connector which would allow easy interchange hydraulically between farm implements and tractors. We suggested that there should be standardization of nuts and bolts. This was not very revolutionary, Mr. Speaker. Everybody thought it was a good idea, but you would have to go to the library to read about it because the government took no action on it. I expect someone will come along to the agriculture committee and suggest they study farm machinery prices. Why? If the house leader is really serious about the use of committees, then he must give the backbenchers that he sends to these committees some assurance that something will be done when their report is made. It can be accepted or rejected, but I will be damned if the government has the right to ignore it. This is what has happened to every committee report that has been tabled in this house.
The committees will have to have a permanent secretariat. I get tired of listening to civil servants telling committees that they cannot do this or they cannot do that; that they cannot tell them how to run their administrations. I think training has to be provided. A permanent secretariat will have to supply translation facilities and legal and research facilities for committee members. When this is done, then I believe that the committee system under our parliamentary structure will perform a legitimate function and not take away anything from anybody. When a committee reports to the house, in my opinion, only the committee report should be discussed. If this is the case, some provision must be made for a minority report because there are two sides to some questions. Most


committees I have attended have hammered out their report, rewritten and modified it to the point where it is acceptable to all, yet a majority report would have been very hard to come by. In some cases, there is a majority report. If these reports are decided upon in the house, then the committee will have served some function.
I think that having members spending eight or 10 hours a week in a committee is a good idea only if there is some end result. If committees are merely a vehicle for keeping backbenchers busy, then I am not going to attend any more committees. If members see no advantage in going to committees, we will never shorten debate in this house. Any time limit set by the government will prove to be a minimum time for debate and the parliamentary timetable will become very full.
Many times, Mr. Speaker, I have had the opportunity of lousing up the government house leader on such questions as an Easter or Christmas recess and on July 1. I have done this not to be obnoxious but with a view to establishing permanent periods for getting things done. I have always felt that the government was being unfair to the opposition in holding a gun at our head and telling us that if we pass certain pieces of legislation we can have an Easter recess, but if we do not we are going to sit here. I remember one year when we even sat on Good Friday because I would not let the house adjourn. This has not happened since; we have always had an Easter recess and I presume that the present house leader wants to carry on that practice. However, Mr. Speaker, we should decide whether we are going to have a summer recess and when that recess should be. We should take into account the school year and other holidays, set the recesses forth in our four-year term, and we should be prepared to work within these periods.
I want now, Mr. Speaker, to say a word or two about estimates before leaving the committee structure. I have been impressed with the reports from the British House of Commons and from the Interparliamentary Union, which have defined the problem of estimates as one that exists in every parliamentary government in the world, including Russia. All have the same problem, a larger volume of business, a bigger gross national product. Every parliamentary government is unable to handle its estimates adequately. It appears the situation will not change and there is not a hope in Hades of examining estimates thoroughly. I am not sure whether we ought to
September 24, 1968	COMMONS
bother with examination of estimates. In England they no longer bother. Sometimes, in this country, we examine estimates after nine tenths of the money has been spent, the idea being under our rules that we must see where the money has gone before we vote the other one tenth. I do not see that we should be any the worse off if we did not discuss all estimates. In England, they discuss the policy behind estimates and government policy surrounding the administration of estimates. They do not discuss the pounds, shillings and pence aspect of each department. Every so often they take one or two departments and examine them in detail, just as we examine some items of expenditure in the public accounts committee. Each department receives close scrutiny probably every seven or eight years.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
In this country we want to make certain that when the public accounts committee reports something to the government, the government acts on the report. When a similar committee reports to the English government, that government must report on what it did with the committee's recommendation. The report must be given within one year. Here we often take no action on any suggestion in the auditor general's report. Sometimes the government acts, and sometimes it does not. The matter often has to be decided by the house.
We must face many problems. It is safe to say that the government may expect co-operation in the changing of our committee structure. Perhaps the government house leader would indicate what his intentions are in this regard. He might say a word on the subjects of committee reports and the role of committees in our scheme of things. He has been chairman of several committees and I have always found him to be fair and reasonable. The fact he is government house leader may change that, so far as the attitude of the opposition is concerned. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) has only recently been elevated, and I am sure that he has not forgotten the frustrations he experienced as chairman of any committee. He must remember that some committee reports evoked no comment from the government. That was not a satisfactory state of affairs.

The government must look at the entire picture, but it must be careful not to emasculate the role of the opposition, because if it does attempt to do so it will gain very little co-operation. Ultimately, the government will gain more by having the co-operation of all members than by trying to force its own way. More is to be gained by agreement between the house leaders of all parties than through the operation of the internal business committee, which really has not been used so far.
Most Canadians welcomed the Prime Minister's announcement that he would attempt to reform parliament. He will find, I think, that the public is not looking for picayune changes. It is looking for major changes, and in this case, as the lawyers say, it is important not only that justice be done, but that it appear to be done.
I wish to say a few words about the subject of televising the procedures of this house. I hope that you, Mr. Speaker, will give consideration to the installation of permanent television cameras in this house. I hope that neither the C.B.C. nor any other network has control of those television cameras. They should be operated as the cameras in the United Nations are operated, and the film ought to be made available to the media at large. I submit that Mr. Speaker ought to be responsible for the administration of this televising in the same way that he is responsible for the verbatim reporting of the debates in this chamber. I suggest this because I have seen occasions in the past when crews of the various news media competed for space, not only in this chamber but in this building. I think newspapermen will agree with me that the television coverage of debates in this house may well modify their reports of those debates printed in newspapers, reports which so far have been exclusively furnished by newspapermen.
I hope you will give consideration to controlling this medium sir, and I hope that we may have an answer on this question from the appropriate authorities soon.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (President of the Privy Council) moved:
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE-PROCEDURES RESPECTING INSTRUMENTS IN VIRTUE OF STATUTES
speechtext:
That a Special Committee of twelve Members, to be named at a later date, be appointed to consider and, from time to time, to report on procedures for the review by this House of instruments made in virtue of any statute of the Parliament of Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could take the few minutes remaining this evening to explain the background of the resolution, for the benefit of hon. members who did not participate in the throne speech debate or who were not present last week.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) has been a student of this question for some years, as have a number of other hon. members in the house including the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). One of the arrangements made to deal procedurally with the problems coming before the house this coming autumn, and in any subsequent period, is the establishment of a committee for the purpose of studying procedures for the better review of statutory instruments, to use the technical term which they are given.
We spend a good deal of time in this house, and, quite properly, in examining details of legislation that is brought before the house, in debating the actual terms of the legislation and in amending legislation from time to time to bring it more closely in line with the aims which the government has in putting it forward or with any purpose which the house, generally, might find acceptable.
A great deal of the legislation which we have seen during our time in the house has contained a provision worded, one way or another, to the effect that for the further and better carrying out of the provisions of the legislation the governor in council is to be entitled to make regulations or orders, or is otherwise given authority to enact what is called delegated legislation, for the better carrying out of the statute.
We find ourselves in the position, therefore, that while a bill may receive intense scrutiny, the application of the bill is left to an administrative body. In fact, measures which may encroach most on the personal privacy, property and rights of the individual may actually be enacted by the administration without any opportunity being given for the elected representatives of the people to give
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Bechard).]
them any direct review. This resolution does not propose to set up a standing committee on delegated legislation itself. What it does propose is that a special committee should be established for the purpose of examining our practice in Canada in this field of statutory instruments or delegated legislation to ascertain whether it would be advisable to set up some kind of procedure so that this house, more particularly through a committee, could make a better scrutiny of these subsidiary instruments by which rights are so much affected. I think there will probably be agreement in all parts of the house as to the acceptability of this motion. I confess that in putting the motion forward at this time we are scarcely engaging in a daring or pioneering step. I note that in 1932 the Senate of Australia set up a committee to review statutory instruments to see how they worked in that country and to study what the procedures were. In 1944, the House of Commons in Westminster set up a select committee on statutory rules and orders and since 1946 that committee, a standing committee known by the nickname of the scrutiny committee, has been charged with scrutinizing this kind of delegated legislation produced by the administration.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
The increased use of orders and regulations has been a necessary consequence of the rapid extension not only in Canada but in all other western countries of government influence in broader areas of the economy and other areas of hitherto private endeavour, in line with the change in public philosophy to a more interventionist attitude. At the same time the standing procedures of the parliamentary system have not been extended to carry forward parliamentary control and our purpose in engaging in this proposed study is to see what might be done to provide continuing supervision of this kind of activity.
Perhaps I might refer to some related questions to make it clear that they are not being dealt with by this particular resolution. One of the means of controlling administrative action to prevent interference with the rights of the individual is of course by providing legal rights of recourse, either by appeal to the regular court system or by means of prerogative writs, where it is felt there has been a denial of what is described as natural law, or, to put it in non-technical terms, where there has been a violation of the ordinary rights of people.
September 24, 1968	COMMONS
This resolution and the committee to be set up will not deal with that subject matter. One of my responsibilities, as President of the Privy Council, will be to suggest further procedures which might be followed for the purpose of reviewing our system of administrative law and the system of appeals we have established. This is a responsibility I share with my colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner). If thought desirable, further means of enabling legal scrutiny of the administrative process will be suggested.
Another institution often discussed in this context is the Scandinavian system of ombudsman. Here again, this resolution does not directly at least involve the recommendation that we set up such an institution in Canada. I think it is fair to observe, however, that the British parliament has decided that a necessary corollary to its select committee on statutory instruments is the appointment of an ombudsman, or parliamentary commissioner as they call him, and they have recently established such a post.
The history of parliamentary consideration of this type of committee has been a long one in Canada. In 1943, the late Mr. Brooke Claxton, then a private member for St. Law-rence-St. George, commented-and I quote from Hansard for that year at page 296:
The practice oi tabling orders in council is, for ail practical purposes, an empty form. I suggest that orders in council be referred to a committee for consideration-not all orders, but orders having the effect of legislation of a general nature.
Another notable Canadian who has shown an interest in this subject is the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) who in 1945 advocated a Senate committee on orders in council to ascertain whether they impinge and infringe upon private rights. Again, in 1949 the right hon. member for Prince Albert advocated the appointment of a committee on ministerial powers to function in the same way as the scrutiny committee at Westminster. In short, what we want the committee to do, is to review what is done under delegated legislation and to recommend to the house the best means of carrying out the will of the people in such a way, as the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) has just said, as to make sure that justice is not only done, but appears to be done.
Perhaps I could call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
